speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
1 rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of press reports that an official of the Department of National Revenue has confirmed that the costs of forms of prostitution are subject to tax write-offs under section 18 of the Income Tax Act as a business expense, and taking into consideration that those who take advantage of this tax break are deriving pleasure at other taxpayers' expense, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt):
That this House directs the Ministers of Finance and National Revenue to launch an immediate investigation into reports that section 18 of the Income Tax Act is being used to write off the costs of pleasures obtained at massage parlours and houses of ill repute as business expenses and that should this be the case, the government should not allow these items to be used for tax write-offs.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF FIRST DOMINION CARILLONNEUR, PROFESSOR PERCIVAL PRICE
speechtext: 1 wonder if I might ask hon. members to join me in marking the presence of a very distinguished visitor in our gallery. On July 1, 1927 the magnificent carillon in the Peace Tower was dedicated and a recital was offered by the first dominion carillonneur, Professor F. Percival Price, who occupied that position from 1927 to 1939. subsubtopic: QUEBEC'S BILL NO. 1-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PROTECT RIGHTS OF ENGLISH MINORITY IN QUEBEC

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: QUEBEC'S BILL NO. 1-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PROTECT RIGHTS OF ENGLISH MINORITY IN QUEBEC

subsubtopic: QUEBEC'S BILL NO. 1-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PROTECT RIGHTS OF ENGLISH MINORITY IN QUEBEC
speechtext: It is the purpose and preoccupation of the federal government that the context within Canada for the survival and flourishing of the French language and culture should be favourable but as I have made clear on every occasion, the federal government does not believe that the English minority in Quebec should be denied access to English-speaking schools.

subtopic: CONSERVATION-HOME INSULATION PROGRAM-NAMES OF PROVINCES AGREEING TO CO-OPERATE
CONSERVATION-HOME INSULATION PROGRAM-NAMES OF PROVINCES AGREEING TO CO-OPERATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It relates to the statement he made last week concerning the government's home insulation program, details of which are exceedingly scanty. In view of the fact that the estimated cost of insulating an average home is $900 and the amount the government proposes to pay is $350, leaving $550 to be paid by the occupant of the house, which will be one of the major obstacles to making this program effective, I want to ask the minister which provinces have agreed to institute loans for the purpose of home insulation. Also may I ask him whether, if provinces do not co-operate in the plan, does this mean that in those particular provinces not even a $350 taxable grant will be available to the residents of that province?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONSERVATION-HOME INSULATION PROGRAM-NAMES OF PROVINCES AGREEING TO CO-OPERATE
speechtext:
Perhaps I should make it clear at the outset that when he talks about the costs of reinsulating a house-the hon. member used such figures as $850 to $950-he is talking about an insulation job which would be done by a contractor. If an individual were to do it himself, it could be done for a great deal less. I believe that $250 to $350 should cover substantially all of the insulation material associated with such reinsulation.
As to the question about the provinces which have indicated they are prepared to add loans, to superimpose loans, or to associate loans with our grant program, that is presently under negotiation with a number of provinces. Ontario is a good example. The province made an announcement about this during the election campaign, but the actual details of that announcement, how their loan program might work, had not been worked out then and I am not sure whether they have been worked out yet. The province of British Columbia did have a loan program which was administered by its public utilities commission. I believe the province of Manitoba had a loan program, and other provinces have been considering it, but this is part of the discussion which will take place between now and the September 1 deadline for the introduction of the program.

subtopic: CONSERVATION-HOME INSULATION PROGRAM-POSSIBILITY OF MAKING EFFECTIVE DATE RETROACTIVE
CONSERVATION-HOME INSULATION PROGRAM-POSSIBILITY OF MAKING EFFECTIVE DATE RETROACTIVE
speechtext:
In
view of the fact that the program does not come into effect until September 1 and since the program can be most effective if work can be done during the summer months, has the minister given any consideration to making the date retroactive so that any individuals who choose, and qualify otherwise, to insulate their homes during the summer months, even if they have to wait until after September 1 to be paid, can do so under the plan, or would the minister be prepared to adjust the
July 4, 1977

plan to do that so that as many people as possible can start insulation at present?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONSERVATION-HOME INSULATION PROGRAM-POSSIBILITY OF MAKING EFFECTIVE DATE RETROACTIVE
speechtext: We did consider that particular suggestion but it was ruled out when a very close examination was made of the administrative complexities that such retroactivity would introduce. We also feel that a period between now and September 1 is a good period for those who would not qualify in the first round. As the hon. member knows, the program will be made available to those who own or occupy houses which are the oldest 20 per cent of the housing stock in the country, and that will take a little bit more than a year to complete. I am sure there are many other Canadians who will want to take advantage of insulation supplies to insulate their houses without the benefit of the loan program because of the savings involved. I would recommend that those persons purchase their insulation during this two month period.

subtopic: CONSERVATION-HOME INSULATION PROGRAM-POSSIBILITY OF INCLUDING TENANTS IN PROGRAM
CONSERVATION-HOME INSULATION PROGRAM-POSSIBILITY OF INCLUDING TENANTS IN PROGRAM
speechtext:
In
view of the fact that there is nothing in this program to assist renters in insulating their residences, as is shown by the program which the government has been carrying on in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia where 40 per cent of the residences were occupied by tenants but 97 per cent of the grants went to homeowners, has the minister any program within this policy by which those who are in rented accommodation, and who need to reduce their energy costs just as much as homeowners, could be assured of assistance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONSERVATION-HOME INSULATION PROGRAM-POSSIBILITY OF INCLUDING TENANTS IN PROGRAM
speechtext: We do anticipate that this will be possible, that renters will be able to take advantage of this program one way or another. We have been criticized in some quarters for trying to intrude into provincial jurisdiction. We have been trying to point out to the provinces, on the other hand, that unless certain actions are taken by them with respect to the landlord and tenants act or with respect to certain rent control practices, there will not be an incentive for the owner to reinsulate his house and therefore provide the benefit to the tenant. That is a very important part of the program as far as we are concerned and we hope the provinces will take the necessary measures to qualify.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF NATIVES FROM AIRCRAFT-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Is he in a position today to make a statement to the House on the very unfortunate incident which occurred at the Ottawa airport? A number of native persons were removed from an Air Canada aircraft
Oral Questions
for the alleged reason that those people were of native ancestry. Serious charges of discrimination have been levelled against the airline. Is the minister prepared to make a statement in that regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF NATIVES FROM AIRCRAFT-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Air Canada has clearly indicated that the ancestry of the group had nothing to do with the fact that there was an overbooking, and certain people, therefore, could not be carried. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 wonder if the minister could tell the House why people who had already assumed their seats on the aircraft, people who had confirmed reservations, were removed in this sorry situation and why people who had not yet boarded the aircraft were not told that the aircraft was overbooked.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF NATIVES FROM AIRCRAFT-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as far as I know at the present time it was part of the routine procedure for dealing with overbooking, but I will be glad to look into that further to see whether there were any special circumstances.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF NATIVES FROM AIRCRAFT-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext: It being apparent that the native persons involved through their national association are seeking redress in the courts by way of charges of discrimination, has the minister sought the advice of the Department of Justice as how the airline will behave in court with respect to this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF NATIVES FROM AIRCRAFT-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext: The Department of Justice would not ordinarily be involved.

subsubtopic: OVERBOOKING BY AIRLINES-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister used the phrase "routine procedure". I hope he does not mean that overbooking is routine, because those of us who travel know that that has become all too prevalent a practice. Would the minister agree that the problem is serious and that something should be done to prevent an airline from overbooking, which in itself is an offence under law?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: OVERBOOKING BY AIRLINES-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a serious problem in trying to have airlines move at capacity while still allowing people to reserve and cancel without notice at no charge to themselves. I have raised this matter with the airline, and I hope that Air Canada and other airlines will seriously consider the possibility of charging for an absolute reservation, a bumpable reservation and the like in order to make sure that people know what it is they are buying.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many long and intensive hours have been devoted by members of this House to the detailed consideration of Bill C-27 both during the hearings of the standing committee and at the report stage. Now that we have arrived at third reading, it seems to me appropriate to set the main provisions of Bill C-27 in perspective. I also think it desirable to take this opportunity of setting the record straight on errors and misrepresentations which have been made about the bill.
The first objective of the bill is to improve the quality of the employment related services of the federal government to Canadians. This is reflected in our proposal to integrate the Unemployment Insurance Commission with the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Undoubtedly, this will help to ensure better access to such services, better identification of needs and a better delivery system through integrated, personalized services in one location under a unified management. The amendments will also provide an improved framework for the achievement of a better balance between service and control in the administration of the unemployment insurance program, and the commission will be reviewing all existing service and control measures with a view to improving them both and achieving an optimum balance between the two. The integration of the two organizations will also promote the development of more pertinent and more coherent employment and income protection policies and programs. In this latter respect, 1 think our proposal to extend the commission form of management, which ensures adequate participation of the
Employment and Immigration
private sector, both labour and management, to the entire spectrum of employment services is particularly fitting.
The second, and complementary, objective of Bill C-27 is to streamline and improve the unemployment insurance program in order to make it more responsive to present economic circumstances. One area of such improvement will be the unemployment insurance benefit structure, which will be simplified and more equitable. It will also be better adapted to regional economic conditions, particularly as a result of the amendment 1 have made to add additional regional extended benefit entitlement in regions of high unemployment. Similarly, the variable entrance requirement will make the unemployment insurance program more sensitive to regional differences. We have been told that a variable entrance requirement is a major departure from the previous so-called concept of equality of access to the program and that it will balkanize the country and threaten its unity. When the NDP opposes the variable entrance requirement, they ignore the fact that workers living in areas of high unemployment face greater difficulties not only in finding employment but also in holding on to jobs. This is indicated in the statistics we have already circulated together with my statement on April 26 showing the higher proportion of short-term attachments in regions of higher unemployment. Among the murky misrepresentations made by members of the NDP on the variable entrance requirement there was one ray of light that came from the hon. member from Brant (Mr. Blackburn). He supported the notion that the entrance requirement could be increased when unemployment decreases. This is, of course, precisely what the variable entrance requirement does.
The representations made by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) on the variable entrance requirement have been distinguished more by their verbosity than by their accuracy. The most outstanding example is the reference he made both during the committee and the report stage to the brief submitted by the Canadian Mining Association. In quoting from the association's brief, he stopped just short of quoting a sentence in the brief which is in full support of the government's position. I think it is essential that the position of the Canadian Mining Association be put on record. The omitted sentence reads as follows:
We believe, therefore, that the 10 to 14 week variable entrance requirement proposed by the minister on April 26th to your committee is appropriate and equitable under existing circumstances.
This is not an isolated example of distortions. The hon. member for Nickel Belt made a statement during the report stage that when he visited the St. John's Canada Manpower centre in Newfoundland, there were only two jobs listed on the job board. This is not so. The manager of the CMC advises that on that day he had upward of 50 jobs listed. Apparently the hon. member visited the office early in the morning and looked at one job board reserved for new jobs listed that day. Other job boards contained listings of dozens of other jobs. In view of these inaccuracies, Mr. Speaker, one wonders at all other statements by the hon. member.

July 4, 1977
Employment and Immigration
The major objective of the unemployment insurance amendments in bill C-27 was not to cut costs. It was to achieve a better allocation of resources. As I stated on second reading, the evidence we have accumulated points to the fact that unemployment insurance is not the most effective way of helping to resolve the problems of those with a short-term attachment to the labour force. This was one of the reasons we substantially increased the funds available in our employment strategy to fund alternative measures, such as direct job creation, training and counselling. It was not, as spokesmen for the NDP have alleged, that we felt that the short term attachments were "ripping off the system".
This brings us to the third general objective of the bill, which is the provision for developmental uses of the UI funds. These are positive steps we propose to take to help reduce unemployment. In the area of training, we will rationalize and simplify the income maintenance arrangements for unemployment insurance claimants taking Manpower training programs. It is well established that suitably designed training programs increase earning capacity and longer term employability. Moreover, the new arrangement will liberate additional funds for training. Yet the NDP by opposing the provision, would deny these advantages to Canadian workers, notwithstanding representations I have received from at least one NDP member that additional training is urgently needed by the unemployed in his constituency.
As I indicated in my remarks at the report stage, the government is fully sensitive to the fact that the use of unemployment insurance funds for work sharing and job creation represents a new departure. I have also indicated our sensitivity to the potential problems involved and to the concerns expressed by representatives of management and labour. Nevertheless, these new approaches seem worth trying since they potentially represent a more positive and creative use of income maintenance funds. The government recognizes that work sharing will not be viable unless both labour and management in particular establishments are prepared to try it out.
I repeat the assurances I have already given to the House, that the provisions relating to work sharing will not be implemented unless such support is forthcoming.
At this point I think it is also essential that the record be set straight on our concept of work sharing. It has never been envisaged as a general way of solving the problems of an over-all shortage of jobs. Rather, it would be designed as a way of helping particular establishments facing temporary economic difficulties to share work for specified periods rather than laying off part of their work force entirely.
I also repeat my assurance that we will undertake further intensive discussions with the new advisory council on the use of unemployment insurance funds in job creation projects. 1 am hopeful that exploration of the problems and how they may best be solved will lead to the conclusion that we should, in fact, proceed on a pilot project basis to determine the extent to

which the advantages we see in these ideas can be achieved in practice.
The amendments contained in Bill C-27 have been made as a result of a long period of investigation, discussion and debate. I am confident that the integration of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Department of Manpower and Immigration, and the revisions of the unemployment insurance program constitute a sound basis for providing better employment services to Canadian workers and employers. I have already mentioned the need to achieve a better balance between service and control in the administration of the unemployment insurance program, which will be promoted with this bill. During the discussions in committee and in the House I have been struck by the frequent references made by many members on the need to provide better service.
In this connection it should be recalled that in the years immediately following the introduction of the new legislation in 1971, the commission's first concern was to improve service. As progress was made in that direction, parallel steps were taken to improve control measures. The commission's continuing responsibility for ensuring the integrity of the unemployment insurance program by maintaining adequate control is doubly important since the commission is the steward not only of public funds but also of premium contributions made directly by the private sector. I am not satisfied that we have yet achieved an optimum balance between service and control. 1 do agree, of course, that there are clear limitations on the extent to which control measures can be pursued. Financial considerations and public acceptance are two key factors which determine the parameters of control measures. At the same time, the integrity of the unemployment insurance program is essential to the program's acceptance by the public.
As I indicated earlier, many representations have been made to me and to the department both from inside the House and from agencies outside. 1 have read and have had summarized very carefully all the briefs presented to the committee, many of which contained excellent recommendations. In some instances, however, these recommendations ran counter to others. For example, in some instances the 10-week to 14-week period was considered too short, and in others up to 26 weeks a year was recommended. So one has to arrive at an appropriate balance in the circumstances, given the fact that this program can only be made to work if it maintains its credibility. That had to be the guiding force in reaching the decisions that we have made in the department. I thank the House for its attention.

Mr. Speaker,
I find myself in an interesting position. The minister indicated that we have spent long hours on Bill C-27 and that we have heard many witnesses by way of petition or in person. I would bring to Your Honour's attention such groups as the Railway Association, the Employers' Council of British Columbia, the United Auto Workers, the Canadian Construction Association, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canada Labour Council, and the National Anti-Poverty Association. All of these organizations, as well as others, had the required
July 4, 1977

expertise which they brought before the standing committee, which enabled us to come to some rational conclusions in clause by clause consideration of the bill. I believe 1 can stand here and express to them, on behalf of my colleagues on both sides of the House, very warm thanks for a job well done in a very complicated and sensitive matter because, as we have been reminded on several occasions, of the one million unemployed.
The minister has indicated the three objectives of the bill. The first is to improve the quality of unemployment insurance, and in this regard he mentioned the merger of the Department of Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. We all know where that idea stems from: it comes from the official opposition. But we are not seeking credit, Mr. Speaker. 1 notice that the minister made no mention of this whatsoever. But we are used to giving the governing party our ideas. They take them and give us no credit for them.
This merger will improve the quality of the service, and now the left hand will know what the right hand is doing. As my good friend, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) said, we in the official opposition have been, on several occasions, a policy bank for the party which is supposed to be governing the country. But we do not mind; this is part of our responsibility which we accept and exercise willingly.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
We do this in preparation to taking over after the next election. That will be my last statement which can go unrefuted. Then the minister spoke about a balance between service and control. When we talk about balancing service and control, we are thinking about equity and justice, because all too often we as members of parliament are made aware of the harassment by and heavy-handed approach of benefit control officers. You are well aware of this, Mr. Speaker, coming from your riding. In your hallowed position you are made aware of the problems resulting from the heavy-handed approach of benefit control officers.
So we must move in and, with the influence we have, try to convince the minister that the Unemployment Insurance Commission should not use methods of harassment, be overzealous or heavy-handed. I hope this is what the minister has been talking about. This is certainly what I would be talking about if I were sitting in his place. However, I had better stop there. 1 have already made my statement in that regard and the minister knows what I am talking about. We are talking about equity and justice when we refer to the balance between service and control.
The third objective the minister spoke about was to relate unemployment insurance programs to economic realities. What does that mean? It simply means that we now have a variable approach to unemployment insurance. Once again I noted that the minister, with his usual charity, singled out the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau). He said that as a result of that hon. member's input the minister is now providing for further extended unemployment insurance benefits. The hon. gentleman even looked across at me and said that the
Employment and Immigration
official opposition in their wisdom and expertise brought forward a solution which he adopted holus-bolus, that is, the variable entrance requirements. We are not seeking any credit for it whatsoever, because as the hon. member for Victoria said, this party is a policy bank for the party that is supposed to be governing.
This is what we are talking about in terms of unemployment insurance programs being in step with economic reality. I will not dwell any longer on variable entrance requirements: we know what this means. It will mean, now, that people on unemployment insurance for the next three years will be able to acquire benefits depending on the rate of unemployment. There will be a change in entrance requirements in accordance with the rate of unemployment from 10 to 14 weeks, inclusive. This is a step in the right direction. As 1 understand it, it will last for three years, subject to the approval of parliament. After the three-year period there will be a requirement for a 14-week eligibility period.
The third objective was the developmental use of funds. There were many comments on the first objective and vigou-rous comments on the second, and on the third objective we ran into a considerable amount of flak. We on this side of the House were certainly concerned about the job training aspect, we were more concerned about the job creation aspect, and when it came to work sharing there was a traumatic atmosphere. This idea was one which both management and labour were very reluctant to accept: they made no bones about that whatsoever. The original purpose of UI was to provide income protection to unemployed workers while they searched for suitable employment. At one time unemployment insurance was protection for unemployed workers, but now we have moved to another area. Remember when it was just for an involuntary lay-off? 1 do not want to become partisan. 1 do not want to have anything to do with these people. They want to pretend to the workers that free rides are available. But, Mr. Speaker, there are no free rides. It is just socialist philosophy that you get everything for nothing. We will have an answer for that in the next election. Some notes on work sharing prepared by my brilliant research assistant revealed some very interesting findings. Both labour and management felt that section 37 could result in disruptive intrusion into the collective bargaining process, and they were uncomfortable with the participation of government in such arrangements. Both business and labour worried about the criteria used to determine which businesses would be eligible. They feared that the work sharing program might be used to artificially bolster inefficient plants. This view was registered with us by all those whose names 1 referred to in my earlier remarks.
It was found there simply was not enough information fully to support the concept as outlined in section 37. In fact, specifically the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen, the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and the Canadian Construction Association pointed out that the experience of the West German government in work sharing was not, to their knowledge, successful. This is the program on which Canadian pilot projects will be based. Along these lines, the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen told us of the experience of some of their members who found that when they tried the short work week, people preferred to work 40 hours or be laid off.
The creation of inefficiency was a common worry of both business and labour, as was the question of handling fringe benefits. I think they were really concerned about the unwarranted intrusion into the collective bargaining process by the federal government. Both sectors found that unacceptable. We tried to delete the work sharing provision after listening to the advice of labour and management in the standing committee. They said that even with using UIC funds for developmental work sharing schemes, experience had shown they would not work.
I must give credit to hon. friends to my left, because they were opposed to work sharing as well. The minister insisted that it go ahead, however. I want his statement on record so

that we can compare what he said today with what he said on June 23, because I caught him out on one statement with respect to job creation. On June 23 he spoke of consultation with the advisory council as well as with management and labour, but today he spoke only of the advisory council and forgot, maybe conveniently, what he had said about labour and management. The record shows what he said on June 23 about work sharing, as reported at page 7069 of Hansard:
In these circumstances I think it is essential to pursue discussions more widely and fully with management and labour to determine whether there is a basis upon which to proceed before we jettison what may be potentially a very good idea.
He did not say "is a good idea"; he said "may be a good idea". Apparently he was not sure whether it was a good idea or not. Maybe that was a slip, and I will not take advantage of it. He went on to say:
I give my assurance to the House that, if this provision is retained, I will not authorize its implementation until I am satisfied that there is a willingness on the part of management and labour groups to participate. On this basis it is my recommendation that hon. members of this House support the provisions in Bill C-27 for work sharing.
With respect to motion No. 18 proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton West and with respect to the evaluation of job creation, that motion would require an evaluation to be tabled within one year of proclamation of Bill C-27. Let me emphasize that it is our clear intention to undertake evaluations of all the developmental uses of unemployment insurance funds, including the job creation proposal. If the minister were to propose an unemployment rate of 3 per cent or 4 per cent, there would be no difficulty on this side. Also, he would find no difficulty if we were to set the premiums based on the rate of unemployment in the area in which a person lives. It is not right to try to sell people on the universality of a plan and then say to them later that it is not a universal plan after all, that participation in the plan depends on the rate of unemployment in the area in which one lives.
Members on this side have written to the minister in a very responsible fashion. I must make the distinction and say "the NDP", since the dragon made that distinction. We in the NDP have written to the minister. We told the minister that the way in which the present Manpower training programs are operated is inadequate. People are being trained for jobs that do not exist. When we visited Newfoundland to look at the unemployment situation in Atlantic Canada, we found that
7260

hairdressers were being produced by the thousand, but no hairdressing jobs were available. That is why we have suggested to the minister that there must be communication between those at the top end of the bureaucracy and those at the bottom who have responsibility for putting this scheme together and administering it. Certainly we do not propose the joining of those two departments.

We look upon Bill C-27 not as just tampering with the Unemployment Insurance Act. We think there is more at stake than the amendments the minister is proposing to the Unemployment Insurance Act. This whole debate is really on the subject of employment for Canadians. I recall the heady days of 1968 when there was a federal election. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was running for his first term as prime minister of the country. Although there were not many promises, there were two things that he said he was concerned about and would work to try to achieve. One was national unity; the other was the elimination of regional disparities.
We can now, with some experience, observe the success of the Prime Minister's efforts on both these fronts. In 1968 the unemployment rate in this country was around 3 per cent. In 1971 it rose to 6.4 per cent. That was the first year of the great fight against inflation. The Prime Minister said that he did not care if unemployment rose to 6 per cent, he was going to defeat inflation. 1 think his words were that he was going to wrestle inflation to the ground.

I understand that was later. At any rate, he did not care if unemployment rose to 6 per cent, he was going to defeat inflation. In 1974 the unemployment rate dropped to 5.4 per cent. The rate at the present time is somewhere around 8 per cent. That is the StatsCan figure and does not include hidden unemployment. StatsCan changed the method of calculating the unemployment rate in this country and in one month cut the unemployment rate in Newfoundland by half; but 8 per cent unemployment in terms of numbers means that about one million people in Canada are unemployed.
The working class people of this country have been used to fight inflation. The government did not care what the unemployment rate was; it used the working class of this country as the scapegoat in defeating inflation. But it seems to me we have not defeated inflation today. If the present rate is projected to the end of the year, we still have double-digit inflation. You notice, Mr. Speaker, how consistently the government uses the unemployed as the scapegoat. Never does it accept responsibility for maladministration of the economy. The government always finds a scapegoat, and the scapegoat as recently as a year and a half ago was the workers of this country. They were blamed for causing inflation because their wage increases were too high and productivity was too low. Therefore, to defeat this psychology of inflation the government had to bring in a controls program. Again it had to find a scapegoat, and now hon. members opposite are all smelling of roses.
The government brought in the controls program which was advocated by colleagues to my right. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) took credit for it, but he is a little more modest than the hon. member for Hamilton West. As I envisage the next election, it will be run along the lines of the governing party wanting to keep controls, and the Conservative party wanting to lift controls. That is the kind of juxtapo-
July 4, 1977

sition that I have in mind for the next federal election. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) says, it will be Tweedledum and Tweedledee. The government has failed on both counts. We still have high unemployment in this country, and we also have high inflation.
What is the word that we get from the corporate sector of this country? Again we look for a scapegoat. What is the message they are putting across? They say unemployment insurance is one of the prime factors for productivity being down; that after all, we are paying people after only eight weeks' employment and that is a drain on the economy. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association told the committee that we had the most generous unemployment insurance program in the world. 1 point out that we also have one of the highest unemployment rates among the industrialized nations of the world. Among the OECD countries we have the highest rate of unemployment of 15 to 25-year olds, something the government should be ashamed of. According to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the program is a disincentive.
Then the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, which represented small business, said that the program was a rip-off. The Employers' Association of British Columbia also told the committee that the program is a rip-off. The Association of Small Businessmen, headed by the famous-or infamous, depending on your view-John Bulloch, also told the committee that the program was a disincentive, a red rooster.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. 1 welcome the interjection of the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) and trust he will get up and make a speech at some point in this debate. I am interested in his comments, and somewhere along the line I am sure I will be able to comment upon them.
The Construction Association of Canada also appeared before the committee and said the program was a rip-off, that the Unemployment Insurance Act is too generous and the participating time too short. All of the groups I have referred to appeared before the committee. Then the minister admitted to me in committee, "Yes, it is a disincentive program; there is no question at all about that". I cannot imagine what goes on on the other side of the House. The government changes one minister, puts a new minister in his place, and suddenly things change. Let me read to the House the comments of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration's predecessor, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), in committee on May 28, 1975. Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that the whole basis for Bill C-27 is a comprehensive review of the unemployment insurance program which was made between January and June of 1974. This is what the minister had to say:
I think it is a bit of a red herring myself. I think there are other areas that have to be tidied up in the act that are far more significant than that favourite whipping-boy of the short-term work claimant.
Employment and Immigration A little later on he said:
The incidence of disentitlement or disqualification, as an effect of failure to meet one's obligations under the act, is lower amongst the group with a minor attachment to the work force as their proportion of the total claims load than those with a long-term attachment to the work force.
After only a year in his job, the present minister discovered that this was a disincentive program. The previous minister was in office for certainly longer than six months and, based on surveys, he had that statement to make. Perhaps he was getting bad advice from the top bureaucrats in his department, because if he felt that the program was a disincentive, that people were taking the program to the cleaners, he should have spoken up and been honest with the committee. One has to assume that he was being honest when he said that. We have to look, also, at what other groups are saying besides the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, as the hon. member for Hastings has pointed out. I should like to refer to the latest report of the Economic Council of Canada which reads in part:
We believe that most Canadians affected by unemployment are well served by the unemployment insurance system and use it honestly-
It would of course be possible to try to eliminate abuses by cutting certain categories of claimants or the duration of benefits, or by extending the period of work, before claimants could become eligible for benefits. But such recommendations could prove harmful to persons most exposed to periodic and genuinely involuntary unemployment.
The minister referred to my comments regarding the Canadian Mining Association brief, a copy of which 1 received from the clerk of the standing committee. 1 should like to read from page 5 of that brief as follows:
The association condemns the abuses which some unemployment insurance claimants have made of the eight-week qualifying period. It is also aware that this period is shorter than that found in all other foreign jurisdictions, while the maximum level of benefits and the time during which they can be drawn are in excess of those found elsewhere. Nevertheless, with close to one million Canadians unemployed, and with most projections, including those issued by the government and its agencies, indicating the situation may worsen, the time is simply inappropriate from almost every perspective to seek a substantial extension, which we would urge in better times, to the eight-week qualifying period.
That is what is in my copy of that brief, and that is the end of the paragraph. I have never found myself in agreement with the Canadian Mining Association. The association indicated that the government ought to spend its time creating and going about doing things in the economy which will spin off the jobs that are necessary for our people. At this particular time in our history the government is coming in with changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act which will create grievous harm for many sectors of the country, especially people who receive lower incomes. There is a high correlation between the minimum attachment, those who are minor claimants, the length of time they collect benefits, and the regions from which they come. You will see the highest correlation between those who are minor claimants and those parts of our country which have the most aggravated unemployment rates.
1 should like to refer to those who were eight-weekers and then went to collect unemployment insurance. In 1976 they collected 21.22 weeks, which is the average for Canada. The

July 4, 1977
Employment and Immigration
eight-week wonder in Newfoundland collected 31.15 weeks of benefits. In Prince Edward Island it was 28.37 weeks. In Nova Scotia it was 19.1 weeks. In New Brunswick it was 30.44 weeks. In Quebec it was 23.85 weeks. In Ontario it was 15.1 weeks. In Manitoba it was 12.2 weeks. In Saskatchewan it was 11.04 weeks. In Alberta it was 10.53 weeks. In British Columbia it was 18.42 weeks. As we go through the nine-weekers right down to the 20 plus weekers, we find this correlation is evident. Where you have a high unemployment rate in the country, you find people have a shorter attachment period to the work force, which reinforces the New Democratic Party's position. Changes at this particular time can only aggravate an already serious unemployment situation in the country.
What was the basis for bringing in the changes contained in Bill C-27? What led them to do this? The previous minister, now President of the Treasury Board, indicated a year ago that he did not go along with this prevalent attitude. I have the suspicion that there is an election in the offing and the government party will have to go to the corporate sector for donations. They will have to show the corporate sector that they are prepared to be tough. One of the issues the corporate sector has brought to the attention of the government is the minor attachment period and the length of benefits.
When the minister first brought in the bill, it changed from 8 weeks to 12 weeks. There was to be no regional unemployment rate. Therefore, he dropped that bombshell on his caucus and all the Liberal party backbenchers from Atlantic Canada got up and said, "You cannot do this; the NDP is going to make flak in the area''. There was a lot of scurrying around, like mice in the pantry, and they arrived at this position of superimposing 54 regions on the country. We have a complicated Unemployment Insurance Act as it is. We recognize the difficulties in the administration of that act. God knows, that particular administration has received enough letters from me. When I took a look at the proposal, I discovered my riding would be region 21. Within region 21 there is a community, Killarney, which is 52 miles from the city of Sudbury, the industrial centre. In the wintertime the unemployment rate is 60 per cent. Because of the high industrial sectors in Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury, the regional unemployment rate is 7.1 per cent. They will need anywhere from 12 weeks to 14 weeks to qualify for benefits.
The superimposing of the 54 regions will create hardships for small communities. When citizens of these small communities become unemployed, the program is administered in a very unfair way, as the minister is aware from the evidence given at the committee hearings. We know the difficulties, yet he proposes 54 regions. I do not think he understands the difficulties which will be encountered and the red tape involved for unfortunate Canadians who become unemployed. What was the rationale? The rationale was the comprehensive review of the unemployment insurance program in Canada. This is the rationale which was prepared between January and June of 1974. It was prepared after personal interviews with unemployed folk and upon what they called in-house data. Well, it

was in-house, outhouse, backhouse, round-the-house, all sorts of data, much of which was highly erroneous.
Take a look at some of the statements made in part "B" of this comprehensive review. It says: "Canada has the fastest growing labour force of any industrialized western economy." Statistics are given from 1961 to 1975, but there are no accompanying international statistics with which to compare the figures. The document states, further: "The labour force is characterized by a high degree of mobility". The basis for that statement is the statistics for separation in one year, 1974, and changes of address in 1971. What a marvellous, up-to-date piece of research upon which to base a measure like Bill C-27 which the Conservative party has the audacity to support! Here is another statement in the document: "High wage increases have exceeded productivity increases." What is advanced as proof of that assertion? A comparison of wage increases in Canada and the United States in one year, 1974. Yet on the basis of such a comparison the minister is telling us, like the blind leading the blind, what a wonderful proposal we have before us.
I now call attention to another statement in the same document where there is reference to the reluctance of Canadians to work at traditional wage levels. What is the proof? A comparison of federal minimum wages in Canada and in the United States in one year, 1974. Then there is a section on what they call the relationship between job vacancies and unemployment. Again, the figures are for one year, 1974. They have the gall to say there were 92,000 full-time vacancies in 1974, compared with 525,000 unemployed. We are given no information about the nature of those employment opportunities. Another interesting section is called "Profile of claims- study and comments". The first heading is "Separations from employment, January to June, 1974" and beneath it: "One in five quits voluntarily and should be watched."
What is the value of that statement, Mr. Speaker? Unemployment in 1974 was the lowest for five years. It was a boom time, when lay-offs were few and jobs were easily found. It was the year when unemployment took a dip to 5.4 per cent. Even expanding the scope of the study for a full year would have given a more accurate picture, because unemployment dropped from 5.5 per cent in January to 4.9 per cent in June. Then it arose again in December to 6.1 per cent. In the same study, under the heading "Profile of claimants", a comparison is made between 8 to 11-weekers and those unemployed after 12 weeks. The figures used reflect only the situation in 1973 and 1974. What are the characteristics in years of high unemployment, like 1971? The figures which accompany the heading "Claimants listed by dependency, age and sex" are taken from only one year, 1974, and again no comparison is possible with a year of high unemployment. In relation to the duration of claims, once again the only figures were taken from 1973 and 1974 to support findings which go into ridiculous detail on the basis of such a small sample.
July 4, 1977

Then we come to a section on "Exhaustees and post-claim behaviour". Here we find a statement that "63 per cent were able to find work within six months of exhausting their claim; this high percentage may indicate a work disincentive in the case of some claimants." So out of a possible six years of operation, only one month was used, April, 1973. This study covered 2,649 people who exhausted their claims that month. They were surveyed six months later to determine whether they had found jobs. The unemployment rate in April, 1973, was 5.4 per cent. In October it was 5.8 per cent. In March, 1977, it was 8.1 per cent, adjusted. What relevance can a job search at a time of easy employment have at the present time when we are experiencing such a much higher unemployment rate?
Further on we find that in connection with the entry on part-time workers, 1,146 people were studied in August, 1974-a very small sample indeed when one is talking about close to a million people receiving unemployment insurance benefits at any one time. But they surveyed 1,146, in August, and August is the time when work possibilities are affected by student employment. Bear in mind, too, that 1974 was a year of relatively high employment, as I have already said.
I turn now to section "D" of this comprehensive review. They must have spent a bundle putting this together, with its flow charts, bloc graphs, etc. Part "D" is "The alternative approach to profile of claimants", and there is a subheading beneath it, "Relative claim rates and cost ratios". The size of the sample is not given. It was taken from one small, special labour force survey dated March, 1975-10 per cent of the sample of 1973 and 1974 files. No comparison was made with figures for earlier or later years.
Then comes a section called "Work disincentives", section "E". This section consists of summaries of seven studies on the effect of the 1971 act. The two studies which are given most space in the review concluded that the 1971 UIC changes had a negligible impact on the unemployment rate. One of those studies indicated that the benefit rate had the most powerful effect on voluntary unemployment. This conclusion is weakened by the fact that the author assumed that all unemployment is voluntary. The other studies done for the Economic Council and for Treasury Board have been judged to contain serious methodological deficiencies.
Consider other sections and the years to which the studies relate. Distribution of total benefits by provinces, 1973. Distribution of total benefits by occupation, 1972, the year after the new act came into being. Distribution of total benefits by industry, 1973. Total revenues by income class, 1973. Under "1" there is a section "Public perceptions of unemployment insurance". There was a survey done in 1975, they said; but, here again, the sample size is not specified and the questions asked are not indicated in the study. The study then considers the benefit structure and increased entrance requirements. This is section "K" of the survey. It describes the three-phase structure and estimates the financial impact of increased entrance requirements and puts forward arguments against
Employment and Immigration
increased entrance requirements as listed. This, Mr. Speaker, is the basis of Bill C-27.
The Conservative members gleefully grabbed at it and said, "This is what we have been asking for". They should be ashamed of themselves. They have reneged on their responsibility as the official opposition of the House, without properly investigating, debating and looking into the legislation that has been brought forward by this government. They do not even recognize when they are being used politically, they are so politically naive. The whole approach to Bill C-27 is, "We said it first. That is what we wanted. We have pushed the government in this direction". The minister, smiling like a Cheshire cat, says, "Come into the trap, buddies. We've got you where we want you".
All they find to criticize is job sharing. What do they pick on? The thing that all groups coming before the committee agreed upon. My, my, what a consensus party it is on my right! The one thing over which they cannot get into hot water is opposition to the work sharing program. We on this side of the House have said to the minister, "Yes, there are times when you can make changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, but you have to base them on the most up to date information and statistics you can get".
1 have tried to point out that this survey, this so-called comprehensive review, is neither comprehensive nor a review. It is a rationale for a decision that has been made which has a political basis. I do not know what infighting is going on in the department. It is not for me to know; it is only for me to speculate about. All I can say is that it is our position on this side of the House that legislation based on information such as this-I have read all the stuff into the record; I have read the review of the Atlantic region, which is outdated-cannot be good.
We in our party have said that we do not object to changes being made to the act, we do not object to tightening up the Unemployment Insurance Act, but before you do it you must concentrate on creating employment opportunities. That is where your first priority should lie. You should not give the impression to the public that you are tough and that you are really getting down to those who are using unemployment insurance as a disincentive, because you are fooling the Canadian public that you are doing something constructive with respect to unemployment insurance and you are sucking in the Tories.
