The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Cullen that Bill C-27, to establish a Department of Employment and Immigration, the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission and the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 and to amend certain other statutes in consequence thereof, be read the third time and do pass.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should have liked to find something satisfactory in the amendments to Bill C-27. Unfortunately those amendments are minor ones and most of them were absolutely necessary as a result of mistakes made in the other legislation. In addition, there is absolutely nothing altering the procedure to establish the insurability of employment. At the present time, unemployed Canadians not only have to experience some difficulties with badly drafted legislation and the reactions of various officials as to their eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits, but they have to accept the decisions of income tax officials who determine the insurability of their job. Let us imagine what goes on. I had to tackle such problems and there are still many which remain unsolved.
Through its investigators the Unemployment Insurance Commission decides whether a job is insurable or not, but it does not make the decision. Quite often they pay benefits for a number of months, even for six months, and then the matter is referred to the income tax people who decide whether the job is insurable or not. After the income tax people have rendered their decision, it takes months and years to be able to go before the Federal Court and defend the position of these unem-
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
ployed. Then it is easy to see that there is no common sense in approving such a piece of legislation.
I have in hand a few notes concerning the piece of legislation which we are debating, to establish a Department of Employment and Immigration, the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission and the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 and to amend certain other statutes in consequence thereof. This is a strange combination of commissioners, officials, advisors who have apparently the responsibility to redefine the tasks and to redirect the objectives to increase employment for the Canadian people. I wish the best of luck to all those who will have responsibilities in these administrative functions, even if this hotchpotch of redefining, of amalgamating is seemingly organized to create a model of confusion 1977, a new style which will perhaps outweigh the confusion reported in history about the attempts to build the Babel Tower. The Department of Transport has already made a demonstration of confusion as far as air traffic control is concerned.
His colleague, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration may entertain the ambition to achieve the same goal on earth, in spite of the variety of factors to be taken into account: a department, a commission, a council, a reorganization of already existing institutions. Let us try and consider the operation of this new department while wishing the planners all possible success.
All that must be based on the most active and the best cooperation of the whole team while assuming it is capable of such cooperation. We already know a team of civil servants who practice cooperation advantageously for the fund. We all know that in the area of income tax, for instance, all kinds of taxes, this team gives us regular demonstrations of cooperation to the extent that even the people find it sometimes a little exaggerated. This laudable propensity to cooperate should be oriented in the field of real advantages, to find for the unemployed the best ways to use their services in order to contribute in their capacity to the production of goods useful to society.
The administrators responsible for that reorganization probably hold several diplomas, perhaps even doctorates, but I shall nevertheless offer advice on the cooperation which must exist between the employees of manpower centres and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. That kind of retraining will require cooperation courses, in order to meet the need to reconcile individual and collective interests. We must take into consideration that those two groups of employees have worked separately for many years. Their managers thought at that time that it was better that way. According to the new plans, they will have to decide together. Let us hope that the situation of the unemployed worker will be better understood.
A real job creation program should be based on the recognition that all forms of socially useful activity deserve to be recognized and remunerated. This would enable us to reach almost everybody except those who are disabled or too old.

July 4, 1977
This could include the mother of a family, for bringing up children in a period of transition is a socially valid occupation. And yet, this occupation is deemed as useful and valid only when the children of other people are involved. Taking care of other people's children, whether as a keeper, a day care attendant or a foster parent may be a source of income. Taking care of one's own children is not considered an employment. This occupation does not therefore entail the right to share in our society's wealth. Cooking meals for strangers is called working in a restaurant, but the cooking of a mother who is preparing meals for her own children is not considered as a job. We are not yet used to the idea that a person may be working without necessarily getting paid for it. We often hear the government talk about guaranteed income, but it shies away from all likely means which might make it possible.
This bill introduces the new notion of sharing work. The government states that the unemployed will not be compelled to accept jobs for which they are not suited, but it is the commission which will define the jobs which it feels is suitable for them. That is a lot of discretion! Because we know already its definition of the word "suitable" and the way it is applied when the unemployed are looking for jobs which are not available, we can foresee what sort of decisions the commission will come down with. Whether a person is young or old, with or without any experience of the labour market, being unemployed is never reassuring. The climate of fear and anxiety which prevails in periods of high unemployment is the result of a great many factors, the most significant of which is certainly financial insecurity. Although Social Crediters are often blamed for talking often about money, ask any unemployed person if it is not money which he is lacking.
The main concern for an unemployed man is to know whether he will be able to provide proper food, clothes and housing for his family. He is also concerned that perhaps he might not be able to cope with problems that could rise suddenly like illness, accidents and so on. With decreased income, he has to meet the same needs as when he had a job, taking into account that there might be delays in the delivery of cheques issued by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. That has happened often, as many of us know. Payments on accounts will remain the same during the unemployment period and, what is more, credit is more difficult to get during that time.
Whatever we say, the many applications to be made to find a job are not pleasant. It should not be left to any employer to take advantage of the situation of an unemployed man to have him do jobs in conditions and at rates that others would refuse. For instance, when forced to give reasonable wages to an experienced worker, the employer would find it profitable to lay-off this older employee to hire a younger one for lower wages. We must consider the fact that this sometimes occurs.
There are also employers who regularly renew their staff because of bad or hazardous conditions. An unemployed man must not be forced to take any job. Generally speaking, an unemployed man who has preferences and requirements about a job finds it hard to get one and moreover he may not qualify
Employment and Immigration
for benefits if he ever indicates his requirements or preferences to the Unemployment Insurance Commission or the Canada Manpower Centre.
Nevertheless, it is not only up to the Unemployment Insurance Commission to determine whether a job is appropriate or not. The civil servants are not the ones who will do the work, it is the unemployed man. Within a reasonable delay, an unemployed man may require the same job he was performing before, as well as the same salary and the same working conditions.
The commission decides on that reasonable delay which cannot be extended more than sixteen weeks in the case of skilled workers and three weeks for general labourers. I repeat that the commission and manpower centres must be aware that consideration is to be given to some factors when establishing working conditions for an employee. It should be remembered that they are dealing with a human being, not a machine, and that the employee can expect security and stability in his employment. He wants his place of work to be well organized and managed. It is only reasonable that he be treated fairly.
He would also like to be informed on the financial situation of the enterprise, so that he could count on an equitable salary. Those are fundamental realities for a human being. Many officials obviously do not consider these factors when it comes to compelling someone to look for a job.
Another factor is very important, and indispensable: the civil servant should be pleasant. Some of them really have a strange attitude. Not all, of course. Someone acts and others react, as if the common tie was not composed of individual assets grouped together, and as if wanting to reform society authorized one to be unpleasant towards its components.
However, I want to point out that the Unemployment Insurance Act has already helped out Canadian workers considerably, as it surely will in the future, provided the errors in the text of some sections are corrected and some planners cease to envisage, in their sick minds, the possibility of full employment at a time when automation is replacing a high percentage of workers in almost every field of productivity. Terms have been sought to qualify various categories of unemployed but that does not improve the lot of the citizen who has no income and no job. While our youth is being encouraged to get degrees, technicians are inventing machines that will create unemployment for our graduates when they leave college.
In a statement on March 15, 1977, the Canadian Council on Social Development was mentioning that many young people are too discouraged to look for a job. When determining the situation of unemployment, Statistics Canada adopts the criterion "actively seeking work" and therefore underestimates the problem. That estimation excludes a great many young people who need and want a job without actively looking for one. According to the 1971 census, 187,000 people from 15 to 19 and 350,000 between 20 and 24 were not included in the official manpower list of employed or unemployed persons nor in that of part or full time school attendance. Many young people have jobs without any qualifications, with poor wages

July 4, 1977
Employment and Immigration
and a limited future outlook. In 1975, 54,000 young Canadians were working half time, not because they chose to do so but for lack of full-time employment.
Surveys made by the Manpower and Immigration Department in 1973-74 showed that a high percentage of young workers, almost three-quarters of those aged 16 to 19 were holding a position with no promotion opportunities, but wished to get one. In the light of these statistics, the board of governors of an organization representing the whole population of Canada criticized the deliberate lack of policies of the federal, provincial and municipal governments with respect to this problem and the general attitude of the population which varies from indifference to apathy and accusations against the young people themselves. The council recognizes that the issue of unemployment among young people is part of the bigger problem of unemployment and underemployment and cannot be dealt with separately. However its seriousness and chronic nature as well as the long term disastrous effects it could have if nothing is done make it a very critical issue from an economic, political and social point of view and we should not forget this.
A detailed analysis of this bill leads us to conclude that the aim of this program is to provide an opportunity for students to get some form of experience and training they will be able to use in the future. The aim itself is quite laudable, but we have to wonder how the government is going to improve the situation if it does not take immediately the necessary steps to ensure some continuity and permanency to this program. It is sometimes difficult to understand the attitude of the government which seems to direct its legislation on unemployment by hiring figures jugglers who do their best to reduce the unemployment benefits by using various means of computing that do not reflect the exact facts concerning unemployment in Canada and above all do not take into account the difficulties encountered by unemployed people who cannot find jobs even though commission officials force them to follow complex procedures based on regulations established by imaginative but unrealistic technocrats. There is no need to have a university degree to know that it is almost impossible to find jobs when the unemployment rate is between 8 to 25 per cent in some areas. All government jugglers should orient their efforts toward job creation instead of doing calculations to reduce unemployment benefits.
On April 14, 1977, the Montreal newpaper La Presse reported the number of unemployed in Canada was dangerously approaching the catastrophic level of one million. Time has come for the government to use every means at its disposal to create jobs and allow those thousands of discouraged unemployed people to get organized to earn a good living honourably. Many suggestions have been submitted to the attention of the government to create long term employment. Some have suggested launching a housing program for the elderly; in rural districts, why not such a home in every parish instead of only one by region so as to use the necessary money to help the disabled, the blind and all those who are physically hand-
[Mr. Dionne (Kamouraska).)
icapped whom we are prone to forget too easily. A great number of practical activities could be created in the field of forest protection and that would contribute to create thousands of jobs during periods when that activity is most needed. It should be possible under shared cost programs to organize reforestation activities to reclaim abandoned farm lands.
Many public buildings could be built-post offices, refrigerated warehouses and how many repairs would have to be made to wharves in several areas! Many wharves on the south shore are drifting away while provincial and federal authorities quarrel about who is going to maintain them and under what terms. I have before me an article published in the local newspaper on Wednesday, June 1, 1977, mentioning that the rate of unemployment reaches 33 per cent in Kamouraska West, and also in another paper, Le Machiniste canadien, of June 1977, under the heading "A big lie", one can read, and I quote:
We have all heard it said that the unemployed are simply lazy people who want to live at the expense of society and the taxpayers. It is a misleading attitude, even if it shared by as influent an organization as the Canadian Manufacturers Association. The reason people are unemployed in this country is quite simply that there are no jobs for them. Government figures prove it.
Statistics Canada published last month a survey showing that in the first quarter of this year there were only 35,400 full time jobs available in all this country and for all classes of jobs. That agency revealed at about the same time that the number of unemployed had "officially" reached 914,000 in April. So there was a gap of 816,600 between the number of unemployed and the number of jobs available ...
And you have Unemployment Insurance Commission officers telling people: Look for jobs!
Even if we admit that there are lazy people, 10,000 and even 100,000, there are still a lot of people who want to work and do not have anything to do. So it is the majority of Canadian unemployed who want to work.
At present, as I suggested at the beginning of my remarks, there is no way a bill like this can be supported. We see from the way it is written how social welfare is increasingly becoming the form of assistance for unemployed workers. Unemployment insurance having changed-not always for the better-so as to deprive an increasingly greater number of unemployed of their benefits by extending the qualification period and shortening the number of weeks of coverage, tens of thousands of unemployed will no longer be eligible for unemployment insurance and will probably go on social welfare.
This clearly discriminatory and disloyal strategy of the federal government will massively affect the population of eastern Canada, Quebec and the Maritime provinces. The compensatory job creation program is still insufficient and insignificant in relation to the considerable savings that the federal government is achieving on the backs of the provinces. The central government is gradually and shamefully transferring its responsibilities for fighting unemployment to the provinces. This transfer of the unemployed maintenance burden is the result of many investigations, but it is still unfavourable to the unemployed.
Among all the lengthy reports that contain all kinds of statistics, I have not seen one about the many cases of unemployed who were not given their benefits because of administrative foul-ups resulting from a badly-made law whose vari-
July 4, 1977

ous sections were re-arranged and written by highly paid technocrats who know nothing about the needs of the unemployed. The high officials, who are never unemployed, use their authority according to theoretical studies of economic mechanisms without taking sufficiently into account the human factors that should be the most important. Oh yes! There has been a lot of publicity about a few cases of fraud. 1 recognize that there can be some claimants who occasionally break the law, but 1 can also prove that, in most cases, it is because of mistakes due to the complexity of the act and the regulations, especially in the case of income earned early during an employment period.
The delay on the part of the commission in sending its weekly reports is one of the main reasons. It is rather easy to see for anyone even remotely aware of the various means by which the law and its regulations are applied. 1 do not understand why people can be inclined to support a bill that will inevitably continue to create a lot of problems in our regions, particularly in those where unemployment is the highest, but of course I guess this is too complicated. However, it seems to me that it would be easy to draft certain texts of law that would be understandable by the people who are unemployed. All these people have not attended university and they have to deal with bills which they do not understand. Besides, there are a lot of civil servants who do not understand them either.
1 remember having put a question to the committee on two clauses of Bill C-229, asking what was meant there. 1 was then answered that it was just legal talk, that those things were written just in case someone would take this issue to the superior court. Then inevitably, if they draft laws such as the one before us, how will it be possible for workers who have to deal with the various problems of unemployment ever to get a little understanding. The Unemployment Insurance Commission has paid out millions of dollars to the unemployed in the course of 1975 and 1976 because there was a lot of unemployment. I still think that the government should rather get itself moving to create jobs. In fact, such efforts are done on a very small scale. Nevertheless, 1 still wish to thank those who contributed in fostering employment in the riding of Kamou-raska with projects under the Local Initiatives Program, or Young Canada Works, Canada Works programs but 1 must say, it is not sufficient in the present situation. We must have other big work schemes. There are a lot of tasks which should be undertaken. 1 have mentioned before certain projects which could be launched, whereby people would get jobs that would earn them an income which at least would allow them to live and sustain their family. I must say that this is the only way of solving the unemployment problem.
It just will not help to give some technocrats and other civil servants very high salaries, which, as I was mentioning before range between $20,000, $25,000, $30,000 and $40,000 a year just to play with the texts of laws which are too complicated. The result of that situation is that you only end up making them more complicated while nothing gets solved. And what are we preparing by doing that, gentlemen of the government? We are just paving the way for revolt. It is sad to say it but if
Employment and Immigration
we do not react by helping workers, we will have to bear the consequences of that inaction.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in our view, one of the most grievous shortcomings of the present government is its failure to recognize the very real seriousness of unemployment in Canada. That failure is demonstrated by the fact that it has scarcely looked at what could be done to solve unemployment. Instead, it has come forward with an amending bill which will make unemployment insurance more difficult for the unemployed to receive.
I hope I do not sound like someone giving a lecture based on past experience, instead of someone making a speech in the House of Commons, but I remind older members of the House, the ones of my generation-there are quite a few-that this country went through an unemployment experience in the 1930s which was indeed tragic. I know it seems that we can have more persons unemployed today than we had in the 1930s and yet not be faced with the almost rebellious and revolutionary situation we faced in that decade. I think one of the reasons is that, after the experience of the 1930s, we won in parliament a good deal of social legislation the result of which is that even in times of unemployment there is money of some sort in the pockets of most people.
That was not the case in the decade of the 1930s. When persons were unemployed then, many of them did not handle any money month after month. They collected vouchers which entitled them to food hand-outs or meals in a soup kitchen. The went to work in my city of Winnipeg in the woodyard. They went out to dig the Grassmere ditch. They were sent to River Heights, to pick dandelions off the grass, in return for which they collected vouchers for food.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: Dandelions make good wine.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext:
That was not so
well known in those days; certainly that was not the purpose. The memories of some members of this House of those days are vivid. Younger members who do not recollect those days, or whose parents did not describe those days to them when they were children, would do well to read a book written within the last decade by James H. Gray, entitled "The Winter Years". That book effectively "tells it as it was".
That tragic decade was brought to an end by the outbreak of World War II. The combination of the unemployment of the 1930s and the following World War led, in the end, to a good deal of social legislation which ameliorated conditions, and still does today. But, Mr. Speaker, we delude ourselves, and this is where the present government is mistaken, if we assume that because there are not unemployed riding the boxcars, because there are not soup kitchens, because there are not riots in places like Regina, because there are not marches on
7268

July 4, 1977
Employment and Immigration
Ottawa, the problem is not as serious today as it was then. I contend that present unemployment insidiously is doing untold damage to the fibre of our people and untold damage to the morale and unity of our country. I argue that the government ought to tackle unemployment seriously; it should not just make it more difficult for the unemployed to collect unemployment insurance benefits, which is all Bill C-27 does.
My recollections of the 1930s were reinforced by an experience which the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow) and I underwent a short time ago. Taking advantage of June 24 being a holiday in Quebec and hence a holiday for the House of Commons, we set up a one-day hearing in our city, Winnipeg, inviting persons, organizations and groups to come before us and tell us about unemployment as they know it. We announced-I suppose that is why so many came-that neither one of us would make a speech.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: You must have had a mammoth crowd.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: Yes, it must have filled a telephone booth.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: We had quite a crowd. We made it clear we were there to listen. We heard from about 16 or 18 delegations during the day. Our sessions were held in one of the rooms of the University of Winnipeg in my constituency. Of the delegations we heard, only one actually suggested that there was no unemployment problem. It was the nurses' delegation, representging the Manitoba Association of Registered Nurses. When I said that, since I spend a good deal of time in Ontario to carry out my duties as a member of parliament, I had heard about nurses being unemployed in that province, the answer was, yes, the association knew that. I was told some hospitals in this province had been closed, which was one of the reasons Ontario nurses were moving out there.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: The hospitals were closed by a Tory government.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext:
But that was the only delegation saying there was no unemployment problem. We heard from various trade unions and varous groups and organizations. But what impressed me most, and 1 discussed it with my hon. friend for Winnipeg North, who will be along later this evening-if he makes the same speech I am making, that does not mean there has been collaboration between us- was the case made to us on behalf of young people. It was made in particular on behalf of two different kinds or groups of young people. On the one hand we had representatives of students of the University of Winnipeg and the University of Manitoba who told us of surveys they had made showing that a substantial number of graduates of last year and the year before had not yet found work. The plaintive case they made to us was that it was damaging and demoralizing for young persons to go to university with the thought of ultimately being able to make a special contribution to society, only to find, on coming out, that there is no place for them.

1 will spell out a bit just how the day ran. We had one university group in the morning, and another in the afternoon. In that way, they did not hear each other. However, both university groups had the same story. They were wondering what was ahead for them and for this country, when there are no jobs for many of those we put through university, with all the years of study and sacrifice that they make. The other group of young people represented at those sessions held in Winnipeg on June 24 was from areas like my own of Winnipeg North Centre and Winnipeg North where many do not get to university. They get through elementary school and high school at best. For them, too, there are no jobs.
We had social workers there, pleading with us to bring to parliament the message that these young people are not just discouraged because there are no jobs, but they are finding their way in increasing number into institutions of various kinds. I remember, in particular, one sister from one of these organizations pleading with us to realize what the unemployment situation is doing to the very lives, character and future of the young people of this country.
I lived and worked through the 1930s. I could not write the book that James H. Gray wrote, but I can certainly tell the story of those days. Some of us came into politics because of what we went through in the thirties. I say what is happening today is worse. In the thirties, the economy had ground to a halt. There were things that could be done to get us out of that. However, if we do not get out of this, if we go on causing young people, whether they are of the upper levels who can get to university, or the levels that do not get there, to find that there is nothing for them to do, God help us in the years and decades that lie ahead.
This is a problem of great seriousness. I see no evidence that the government across the way appreciates that seriousness at all. I said a while ago that in my view unemployment is not only damaging the fibre of our people as individuals, but it is doing great disservice to the morale and unity of this country.
1 hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will not think I am getting into tomorrow's debate. That will come. I am talking about unemployment and unemployment insurance.
One of the major reasons there are stresses and strains in the Canadian confederation is the economic conditions. When unemployment is as high as it has been for a long time in the province of Quebec, one cannot blame the people of Quebec for wanting a shake-up, wanting something new. When unemployment is high in the other parts of Canada, the people in those parts look for someone to blame. The tendency has been around for a long while to blame the other group, the other racial division. That has been exaggerated because of the unemployment that is. there. If we really want to save our country tomorrow, we must do more than our dedication to a national and united country. Let us not indulge in platitudes and speeches, thinking that the language issue is the only issue. The fundamental issues that disturb the people of this country are the social and economic bread and butter issues. I do not
July 4, 1977

see any evidence of the government realizing the seriousness of the situation.
1 plead as strongly as I can with the government to realize that this is not something that is passing just in 1976, 1977 or 1978. It is not something that is so much less worse than unemployment in the thirties that we do not need to worry about it. The future of life in Canada, the future of our country, can depend very largely on whether we can find socially useful and productive employment for all the people of this country.
My friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), in the better part of his speech had a good deal to say, with which I thoroughly agree, about the loss that we suffer every day that nothing is done about unemployment. He cited the millions of dollars that we lose every day, not just in terms of the money that is being paid out in unemployment insurance but in terms of the production that is not produced. This country still needs housing on a massive scale. This country still needs urban renewal in all the cities of Canada. This country still needs modern and efficient transportation systems across the country and in our urban centres. These things call for employment in excess of the numbers that are unemployed today. For the government to sit there and try to run the country, when it cannot find a way to put together people and resources to produce those things that are needed, is a sham, and that government ought not to be sitting there today.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext:
1 plead for serious consideration of the most effective answer to unemployment which, in the simplest terms, is employment. In the simplest terms, it is to put the country to work producing those things that our people need.
Hon. members are quite used to hearing my voice concerning all aspects of pension matters. One of the things that I plead for is the possibility of earlier retirement. 1 do not ask that it be made compulsory, not in the least. However, I firmly believe that if pensions such as old age security and the Canada Pension Plan were made available on a voluntary basis at age 60 instead of age 65, many of our workers would take advantage of that opportunity. There are many jobs where one does not want to quit. I am an example of one who does not want to quit.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: What about the Senate?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext:
Forget that. That is not work. It is one thing, at my age of 69, to enjoy being in parliament. It is another thing, at age 50, 55, 58 or 60, to go day after day into the rolling mills, railway shops, mines, textile factories, packing plants or forests and do backbreaking work. On occasion I talk to workers at the shop gates. They put many things to me, but the thing that is spoken to me most about is earlier retirement so that they can escape from the rat race and have a chance to live.
Employment and Immigration
All power to those who have the kind of job where they can stay on, but I suggest that it would be a practical, positive solution for a goodly number of our unemployed if earlier retirement were made possible. But can we get these people across the way to take a look at this proposition? No. They say we are trying to force people to retire, instead of making it voluntary. They say that the country cannot afford something for those between 60 and 65 because there are others below 60 who are having a hard time. Granted there are these kinds of problems, but is the government examining them? No. Its answer to unemployment is to make unemployment insurance more difficult to get. Hon. members opposite say they are responsible. They say they are the government of the country and that they are running it. They are running it into the ground.
A while ago my hon. friend from Kamouraska referred to the guaranteed annual income-something else that we on this side of the House are proclaiming-and suggested it was one way to answer unemployment, that it was a real way of sharing available work, and that it was a form of security. But can we get the government to examine this? No. It has to be discussed with the provinces, says the government; the provinces do not want it, and so on. These so-and-so's across the way are presiding over a country rich in natural resources, rich in real wealth, rich in people who are prepared to work. Yet they cannot somehow put things together so that goods can be produced to provide a guaranteed income for all our people, to provide for voluntary retirement, and to provide for the production of those things which our people need.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: They would like an election, Stanley. That is all they think about.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that what those across the way want is an election. The only reason they want an election is that they think that can put them back in office for another three or four years.
I have already mentioned my age, Mr. Speaker, which simply tells you how many years 1 have had to endure this country under a Liberal government, the kind that keeps fooling us about what they are going to do, from Mackenzie King on down, and never really coming to grips with the problems and issues that face us. 1 submit that we never had a better example of that than we have today. Here is this tremendous social problem, the tragedy of unemployment which is hitting our people, yet the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) brings in Bill C-27, the only effect of which is to make it more difficult for unemployed people to collect unemployment insurance. It makes it more difficult in a number of ways. The most serious way of all, of course, is that it increases the number of weeks which a person has to be attached to the labour market in order to collect unemployment insurance, at a time when in some parts of the country it is difficult to get any attachment at all. The government has also built up a complicated mass of machinery for running the program which is bound to take first prize for the impossible.
7270

July 4, 1977
Employment and Immigration How the government has any moral right to stay in office, Mr. Speaker, 1 simply do not understand. This is why I stand here today pleading with the House, and particularly with the government, to take this issue seriously. This is not something which is simply passing. It is not just the experience of the 1930's on a lesser scale. It is a tragic thing which is doing damage to the character and the fibre of our people. It is doing damage to the morale and the unity of our country. I feel very strongly that something better than this bill should be brought in.
In the meantime we have the bill in front of us. I know it has been debated at length at second reading, in the standing committee and at the report stage, but it still has in it these provisions which make it so difficult for unemployed persons to collect their unemployment insurance. There are a number of clauses in the bill that ought to be reconsidered by the standing committee, though even that is not enough. No matter how good an unemployment insurance bill is brought in, it would not be enough. We need other things too, such as production, employment-a whole host of pieces of social legislation. But at least we ought to reconsider this change from an eight week attachment to 14, with a sliding scale and all the complications.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, because I believe we should still review this whole bill, and because in particular I think the bill should be sent back to committee for a reconsideration of the attachment clauses, which make it more difficult to qualify for unemployment insurance, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That", and by substituting therefor the following words:
"Bill C-27 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration for the purpose of reconsidering clauses 29 and 30 thereof."

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the amendment just proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to Bill C-27, which deals with amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. We in the New Democratic Party have fought this bill in the House and in committee because we believe it does a serious injustice to the one million unemployed Canadians.
The bill is a sham in terms of government seriousness regarding the plight of the unemployed. It is an attempt by this cruel and heartless Liberal government to make the unemployed of Canada the scapegoat for the government's own economic failings. No responsible member of parliament elected by his constituents to stand up for their rights, whether they be employed or unemployed, can support this iniquitous legislation which fails to address itself to the nature of our unemployment and to the reason why the people of Canada who want work cannot find it. Rather than assist them in their hour of need, this will only discriminate against them.
If the amendments in this bill are passed, we are going to throw an extra quarter of a million, perhaps even one third of a million, Canadians off the unemployment rolls. This bill will lengthen the qualifying period for a person to become eligible

for unemployment insurance. In view of the unemployment rate of 8 per cent and the lack of job creating policies on the part of this Liberal government, the situation can only get worse. As people become unemployed the government has the nerve and callousness to disqualify them from receiving benefits which they have contributed to over the years.
We hear from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that what is at issue here is leadership in this country. I ask the Prime Minister and his Liberal supporters: where is the leadership in creating jobs and reducing unemployment in the kind of approach we see before us in this bill? Instead of attacking the number one problem of unemployment, this bill attacks the unemployed, and we in this party will not stand for it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext:
The minister tries to do the double shuffle by appearing to be active in trying to change this bill and attacking the problem of unemployment. He said that there are a number of Canadians today who are not really serious about working, that these people move in and out of the work force on a temporary basis, that these people really do not need the extra money, that these are not long term attachments to the work force and therefore are artificially pushing up the unemployment rate and proving to be a drain on unemployment insurance funds. That is the type of rationale behind this bill, that unemployment is really not that bad. To prove it, the government wants to disqualify a number of people from receiving unemployment benefits. 1 reject that kind of argument.
In the past I have risen to try to bring forward statistics from government agencies which refute the claim that people who work eight weeks and draw unemployment insurance are really only minor attachments who are not serious about long term employment. When we look at the problem of the unemployed today and try to analyse who the unemployed are, we receive very revealing facts and figures. Of the one million unemployed in Canada, the shocking fact is that 48 per cent of those people are under the age of 25 years. In other words, the future generation, those we have supposedly educated and trained and will rely on to keep the country going in our old age, make up approximately half of our unemployed. This has got to be a serious problem, not only from the viewpoint of over-all statistics. What is this doing to the future of this country? It is disillusioning the people we will be relying on to keep this country great.
One of the reasons I left the teaching profession to enter politics was what 1 saw happening to some of the senior students I taught. These students had great potential to go on to post-secondary education, but they were not going on to universities or community colleges for job training because they saw some of their friends, who had gone on to university, graduating and not being able to find jobs commensurate with their training and, in some cases, not being able to find jobs at all. At that time I felt if that situation were allowed to continue and grow worse we would be building a generation in
July 4, 1977

this country who were becoming disillusioned about the system and the manner in which the government was operating. In the five years since I have been here, I have seen that situation worsen under the economic policies of this Liberal government.
When the young become disillusioned and when the whole concept of work becomes a foreign one, because people cannot find jobs, then the country is in serious trouble. Yet the government cannot seem to recognize that young people today do not want to go to university and their parents and they themselves do not want to spend hundreds and thousands of dollars getting that kind of training, only to find there are no jobs available when they graduate.
What kind of response do we see? Instead of a commitment to reduce unemployment and to provide jobs for these young people, under the callous leadership of the Prime Minister we hear the government saying to the young people: "Well, you can leave the country". That is the type of response we receive to the problem of unemployment for the young and, in an even worse sense, it is found in this bill.
Because of high unemployment, young people today have not had a chance to contribute for eight weeks in order to qualify for unemployment insurance should they be laid off, which in all probability will happen as long as this government is in power, and that qualifying period is going to be increased to anywhere from 10 weeks to 14 weeks.
All we receive from the federal Liberals are token responses to the problem of unemployment. We get Opportunities For Youth Programs and Local Initiatives Programs. Those programs only provide temporary part-time work at minimum wages, and thus fail. Then the government comes up with new names such as Canada Works and Young Canada Works, which also will only provide temporary make-work projects.
Another response of the government is to create the myth that 6 per cent or 7 per cent unemployment is natural in this country and not serious, as women and young people make up a large proportion of the unemployed. It also tinkers with the unemployment insurance system to make it appear that the government is trying to do something. Another more insidious method is to tell the public that it has to live with high unemployment in Canada, which is somehow indigenous to our country and that the problem is too big to solve. In this bill, that is recognized by the action of disqualifying people, who want to work, from receiving benefits when through no fault of their own they become unemployed.
1 reject the underlying philosophy, exhibited in this bill, that nothing of any real substance can be done about unemployment. Other industrialized countries in the western world, such as France, Japan, Britain, Sweden and Germany, between the years 1962 and 1973, had an average unemployment rate of 1.8 per cent. During that same period of time Canada had an average unemployment rate of 5.1 per cent. I have to ask myself why it is that other countries can do something about the high rate of unemployment but under the Liberal government Canada cannot. I reject the argument that nothing can be done, except to tinker with unemployment insurance or to
Employment and Immigration
implement temporary make-work programs such as Canada Works.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ETC.
speechtext:
Other countries can do it. Surely there is enough competence in this country to do it, but obviously it is not going to be found on the government benches. The government says we cannot afford the cost of full employment programs. I say we cannot afford the cost of high unemployment which amounts to billions of dollars in lost goods, services, taxes, and unemployment insurance payments.
The major problem affecting national unity is unemployment. Look at any of the surveys carried out in Quebec and you will find that the major concern of Quebecers is unemployment and the failure of the federal government to show a meaningful presence in the economy by creating jobs. No wonder the Quebecers are disillusioned with the federal system when they see that the government has consistently allowed unemployment in the province to be higher in Quebec, comparably, over the years than in other provinces.
If we were to reduce unemployment by 350,000 we would add more than $6 billion to the gross national product, a sum equal to the cost of five Olympic games. I am arguing that we must create jobs rather than engage in the kind of nonsense we see in the bill before us. The government should be addressing itself to changing the structure of our economy to one which perpetually creates high unemployment. If other countries can bring down their unemployment rates by restructuring their economy, we can do so.
We shall never solve the unemployment problem as long as we continue to be dependent upon the export of raw materials as opposed to processing and manufacturing here. I come from a region in Northern Ontario where we are blessed with large supplies of raw materials. But I see what is happening. We are digging out our minerals and chopping down our trees and exporting the raw materials to other countries. As we do so, we export jobs, because the jobs are where the material is refined and processed. As long as we allow this to continue we shall remain hewers of wood and drawers of water. If the government were serious about restructuring this aspect of the economy, we could create jobs here at home. Instead, the government allows foreign-owned companies to buy up our minerals and forest products and export them to other countries so that the parent corporations can enjoy the benefits of manufacturing the finished goods.
Is it any wonder that today, because of the policy followed by successive Liberal governments, 60 per cent of our manufacturing industry is foreign-owned, and that over 95 per cent of our oil industry is foreign-owned? When foreign direction exists to such an extent is it any wonder we should continue to export our resources and, in the process, to export jobs ? Is it any wonder that when there are economic problems affecting parent companies in the United States the first lay-offs should affect Canadian subsidiaries? Is it any wonder that virtually

July 4, 1977
Employment and Immigration
no research and development is being done in Canada, with the result that our own research scientists and university graduates cannot find jobs here? Until we tackle the issue of foreign ownership we shall not be able to restructure the economy in such a way as to reduce the exporting of our raw materials, and jobs with them.
Instead of tackling unemployment by ending programs which have created it, such as the anti-inflation program, the government insists on continuing them. The anti-inflation program has taken hundreds of millions out of the pockets of wage-earners. Is it any wonder that we find ourselves in a situation in which factories have to reduce production because fewer people are buying goods? Is it any wonder that factories today are operating at only 83 per cent of capacity, or that they should be forced to lay off employees, with the result that unemployment worsens? We contended when the government introduced the anti-inflation program that it would only increase unemployment. Today this is apparent, but the program goes on nevertheless. What is the response? It is to tinker with the unemployment insurance system, making it worse, to give the appearance that the government is trying to do something about unemployment.
Supporters of this bill are failing to recognize that the number one problem facing this country is the shortage of jobs. We in this party will continue to oppose these amendments because they make it even more difficult for the unemployed to survive. If these people are disqualified their only resource is to starve in the streets or get assistance from municipal welfare, throwing an increased burden upon municipal governments which have the least ability to raise funds.
We want to see changes in the unemployment insurance program but, more important, we want to see increased employment opportunities.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we adjourned for the dinner hour I was addressing myself to the amendments before us in Bill C-27 to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, and I was developing the argument that the government, rather than addressing itself to the fundamental and pressing problem of unemployment, preferred to tinker with the unemployment insurance system.
I was trying to outline why 1 rejected many of the arguments the government was putting forward to justify these changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act which will affect the unemployed at a time in our country's history when they are least able to defend themselves, at a time when our unemployment is as high as 8 per cent, and the projections are that it will be higher. I was pointing out that, rather than tinkering with the system, we need some fundamental changes in the structure of our economy to get away from always developing and exporting raw materials instead of processing them here in Canada, and that we should end the anti-inflation program which has created higher unemployment through
July 4, 1977

lowering demand in the economy by rolling back workers' wages.
1 also want to stress that the government should be taking initiatives in the public sector that have some meaning in terms of job creation, that it should be undertaking some projects which meet direct human needs which the country is facing at this time. 1 can think of programs that we implemented back in 1972 when we had a lower unemployment rate and yet the government, because it was a minority parliament, found the money to institute needed capital projects for municipalities. I think of the construction of sewer and water mains, roads, transport facilities, and aid to institutions such as hospitals. These are areas in which there is a genuine need today to provide services and amenities, and yet we still have one million Canadians unemployed and a government that prefers to tax workers with higher unemployment insurance premiums rather than commit itself to some of these effective capital works projects that provided people with work in the past and provided the general public with needed services.
At a time when there is one million unemployed, the government cannot tell me that it has no precedent on which to base some kind of job creation program. 1 am not talking about the namby-pamby Canada Works projects that it keeps coming up with, or some of the provisions in the bill that we discussed earlier, such as work sharings to which the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) referred. At a time when the majority of Canadians do not have adequate shelter, the government should be doing something about high unemployment by instituting a housing program of some substance. To inject more funds into that would return to the federal Treasury funds ten-fold over as workers got back to work and carried their fair share of paying taxes and spending on goods and services. A housing program that would be meaningful is needed desperately, and it would provide jobs. We also know there are many homes needing repairs and renovations. We know that government assistance in urban renewal is needed. Municipalities have been begging the government not to cut back on urban programs but to maintain adequate funding and, indeed, to increase funding in that area. Yet we get a negative response.
I cannot allow the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) to say that there are not ways to create jobs through the public sector. We know of instances in the past where there have been programs to develop parks, environmental clean-up programs and energy conservation programs, and programs like that could be undertaken now to a much greater degree than the phony and hollow program the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) announced recently. Programs for community services would not only provide services but also jobs.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) mentioned the idea of voluntary retirement at age 60. This would make new jobs available for people in the work
Employment and Immigration
force. Let us not accept the argument that unemployment is such a big problem that it escapes solution.
I pointed out that Canada has the worst unemployment record in the industrialized world. Through imaginative programs in the public and private sectors other countries have been able to reduce unemployment significantly. I categorically reject the negative thinking and the bankruptcy of ideas that the federal Liberals have imposed upon this country and upon the one million unemployed. That is not economic leadership, that is a rejection of the fundamental idea that a government has a responsibility to the people to create and maintain a sound economy.
We in the New Democratic Party feel that this bill would discriminate against the unemployed in the areas of the country where it is virtually impossible to find long-term work. It is no accident that in Atlantic Canada, Quebec, and northern Ontario there is a lack of long-term jobs. That lack exists because of the nature of the regional economies of those areas.
I have been to Atlantic Canada; I come from northern Ontario, and I know what I am talking about. The figures show that in these regions those who can find temporary work are seasonally employed people. In Atlantic Canada, for instance, they work in fish plants for certain amounts of time when those plants are operating, or in some of the woodland operations, or in service industries. In areas like that where the economies are chronically weak, no matter how people try, they cannot find long-term work.
What does this bill do? It raises the qualifying period from eight weeks of employment before a person becomes eligible for unemployment insurance if he becomes unemployed to anywhere from ten to 14 weeks. We have pointed out that that kind of modification will throw anywhere from a quarter of a million to a third of a million people off the unemployment insurance roll and will force them on to municipal welfare rolls because, contrary to what the minister says, these are not people who are just marginally attached to the work force and who really do not need to work. These are young people looking for their first jobs or for jobs to finance higher education. They are women who have been forced to go out to work to supplement their family income because of the government's failure to keep down rising costs. They are people who have to work because their families depend on their incomes, and for the government to disqualify those young people, those women and those unskilled workers, when we have high unemployment, is cruel, heartless, and totally unjustified.
On the average in the Atlantic provinces and in Quebec, excluding the city of Montreal, we find that the requirement before one can become eligible for unemployment insurance benefits will be about ten weeks of employment. In Ontario it will range anywhere from 13 to 14 weeks. In my part of the province, northern Ontario, I suspect it will be about 13. On the prairies it will be about 14 weeks, and in B.C. 10 or 11 weeks. The hon. member for Nickel Belt pointed out that when the government institutes these 54 regions with their varying periods of qualification, there will be a bureaucratic nightmare. We already have problems with the Unemployment

July 4, 1977
Employment and Immigration
Insurance Act as it is. When we divide the country into 54 regions, we will run into problems with people moving from one region to another.
I predict that this minister will have to hire more civil servants to make the already overgrown bureaucracy in his department even fatter. Worse than that, we will have an unjustified application of this act because we know that even within a region there will be differences. In Sault Ste. Marie there may be an unemployment rate of 7 per cent, but in the town of Blind River just a few miles away there might be unemployment rates of anywhere from 14 per cent to 20 per cent. There are regions like that all across Canada. People in towns which have chronic high unemployment are going to be caught by this increased qualifying period, and they will not be able to find jobs. They will be thrown off the unemployment insurance rolls and forced on to city welfare rolls.
This is a bad piece of legislation. It does not attack the fundamental problem of unemployment. Indeed, it attacks the unemployed. I know the minister likes to present the argument that the people who are going to be affected most are young people and housewives, those who really do not need to work, according to the minister. However, his own statistics gathered by his department and by Statistics Canada prove the contrary, that people who are eight to 11-weekers, those who can find only temporary work, are not the majority of those who are claiming unemployment insurance benefits. The minister tries to make the public think that this is a great number of people and that these are the groups who are draining the unemployment insurance fund, milking it and cheating it. That is just not so.
When we look at the statistics on the operation of the unemployment insurance system we find, for example, that in the first five months of 1976 those who worked eight to 11 weeks made up only 15 per cent of all the beneficiaries of unemployment insurance. That is not the great majority. The minister says that even if the figure is only 15 per cent, those people are not serious about working. He says they are in and out of the labour force trying to make a fast buck, and then drawing benefits.
In the first five months of 1976 63.8 per cent of all eight to 11-weekers in the work force were in Quebec and in the Atlantic provinces, areas with low job vacancy levels and histories of only seasonal work. They are not just housewives and young people. Many of them are adult males and heads of households who have to depend on unemployment insurance to keep bread on the table for their families because they can find jobs lasting only eight to 11 weeks, seasonal work. They have to depend on unemployment insurance benefits because of the government's mismanagement of the economy.
If that is not enough to convince the minister, we find that more men than women will be affected by this change in the Unemployment Insurance Act. To the argument raised by the Conservatives that the main beneficiaries of the eight-week attachment period were women and young people, riot serious

participants in the work force, the former minister said at the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, on May 28, 1975, as recorded at the bottom of page 19:18:
I think it is a bit of a red herring myself. I think there are other areas that have to be tidied up in the act that are far more significant than that favourite whipping boy of the short-term-work claimant.
Earlier, speaking of the eight-week attachment period, he said:
The incidence of disentitlement or disqualification, as an effect of failure to meet one's obligation under the act, is lower amongst the group with a minor attachment (eight weeks) to the work force as their proportion of the total claims load than those with a long-term attachment to the work force.
I refer to the following figures again only because I know the minister has a hard time understanding them. In June, 1976, only 12'/2 per cent of unemployment insurance recipients were under 20 years of age; adult women made up 41.7 per cent of recipients, and adult men, 45.8 per cent.
Moreover, let no one accept the phony argument that of the women who collected unemployment insurance benefits, there were some who did not need to work to support the family. A study of unemployment in the years 1971 and 1973 found that unemployed wives tended to come from families with low incomes-women who had to work to meet the family bills, the higher food costs, higher clothing costs and higher energy costs.
This party argues that the proposed changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act to increase the qualifying period will hit hardest the young people and women who need to supplement the family income; they will hit hardest at areas of chronically high unemployment such as Atlantic Canada and Quebec and will not help the unemployed, as the minister likes to claim, by saving money that could be directed into other programs. The changes would just take money away from the unemployed in one area to help the unemployed in another and, in our opinion, that is no way to tackle this crucial problem.
I have tried to outline ways the government could act to create jobs. I have tried to show how this act will be discriminatory. It will hurt the unemployed, especially in regions where people cannot find long-term work. For these reasons this party will fight the bill to the end and try to convince the minister that this is not the approach he should take. He should be creating jobs, not attacking the unemployed.

Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) gave notice of changes to this act in December, 1976, the Minister of Labour for the province of Nova Scotia was quoted on the front page of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald as saying that such a move at this time could impose serious economic hardships in Nova Scotia. He said that the timing was wrong, that many people who wanted jobs could not get them, that the real unemployment figures were soaring and not just because people did not want to work. He also said that the provincial social services department would have to pick up
July 4, 1977

the slack for many jobless people left without UIC payments under the proposed changes. He is a Liberal, but was advancing an argument that this party has used in this House and which was repeated this afternoon in the speech of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez).
We find it incredible that at a time of the highest unemployment since the depression, this government attacks unemployment by proposing a change in the eligibility for benefits, thus indirectly attacking the unemployed who need help the most.
Members from northeastern New Brunswick where 25 per cent to 30 per cent unemployment is normal, from Cape Breton as 1 am where 20 per cent to 25 per cent unemployment is normal, or from Newfoundland where most areas except St. John's are equally affected, are all appalled that at this time, when this nation has such high unemployment, the government would be so heartless and cruel as to offer these changes as a means of alleviating the problems which affect the poor and the low income groups.
This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) described the depression and its effects upon the people. Although he did not argue that unemployment is felt as severely now as then, he said that in many ways the effect could be worse because if unemployment amongst the younger generation keeps increasing we will in effect be sitting on a tinder box. We are alarmed at the composition of the unemployed in this nation and the growing unemployment amongst young people-the minister had the nerve to refer to them as kids-young adults graduating from high school ready to enter university, vocational or technical schools at a time when all these institutions are increasing their fees. Both parents need to work to meet the increased cost of living, and the consumer price index is rising to a higher level than was anticipated by the Anti-Inflation Board even four months ago.
The path we are following could easily lead us to doubledigit inflation by next new year yet all the government offers at this time to low income people is a proposal to tighten eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits.
The reason there is so much unemployment in Canada today is basically because there has been less than 5 per cent growth in the gross national product for three years in a row. 1 know the minister and his cohorts who draft the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act do not like to hear us quote the Economic Council of Canada. The basic reason is that we had 3.2 per cent growth in 1974; the rate went up .6 per cent in 1975, was 4.6 per cent in 1976, and right now, according to first quarter figures and the report of the Conference Board, we shall be lucky if we see a growth rate of 4 per cent, a rate which will not even absorb new entrants to the labour force. Therefore one must conclude that unless we can keep young people in school longer or use gimmicks to keep them out of the labour force, unemployment this winter will be between 8.5 per cent and 9 per cent. The ones hardest hit will be young adults, and married women who must work to supplement the family income.
Employment and Immigration
The minister and hon. members opposite who spoke put forward a naive philosophy in support of this bill. Mr. Speaker, the proposed changes in eligibility will affect kids and housewives they say, but I say these are young adults and housewives who must work. If the head of a household earns $25,000 or more, there is no need for the wife or married partner to have a secondary attachment, or marginal attachment as the minister calls it, to the labour force. That family can maintain a decent standard of living. But if the head of the house is making less than $20,000 per year, the married partner must work in order to maintain a decent standard of living. Some call that materialistic. When our middle or upper classes want to improve or maintain their high standard of living, we do not say they are materialistic; therefore why should we accuse people earning between $12,000 and $14,000 a year of being materialistic if they want to aspire to a decent standard of living?

speechtext: And I say nothing of the 20 per cent of Canadian families who live on a measly $6,000 or $7,000 a year.

speechtext: The working poor.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, the working poor and the poor. This bill neglects them. Instead of changing the act, the government should change its policy, to provide jobs in this country.
The growth figures I mentioned previously show that at least 2 per cent or 3 per cent of Canadian unemployment is due to deficiency of growth, or what economists call deficiency of aggregate demand. In plain words that means there is too much unused factory capacity in this country. We underutilize our manufacturing sector and underutilize our human beings, as one can readily see from official unemployment figures. Those figures say nothing of the hidden unemployed. There may be between 200,000 and 400,000 more unemployed than our official figures show, depending on whose figures you accept. Our statistical unemployment figures do not reflect accurately our underutilization of human beings. Mr. Speaker, underutilized human beings and underutilized economic capacity are the main reasons for much of our unemployment.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) brought down his budget recently he said implicitly something the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had said explicitly, namely, that our people are trying to take too much out of the economy. He tried to recite the classical formula of inflation, too much money chasing to few goods. He used a monetarist argument which bears little relationship to our economy which suffers from the underutilization of human beings and factory capacity. Mr. Speaker, if it were a fact that Canadians are taking too much out of the economy, our factories would work at 100 per cent and unemployment rates would be in the vicinity of 4 per cent or 5 per cent. But that is not the case. Our unemployment rates are in the 8 per cent to 8.3 per cent region and, if the projections of the Conference Board based

July 4, 1977
Employment and Immigration
on first quarter figures are correct, this winter unemployment could go up to 9.0 per cent.
The minister, and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), have suggested that we oppose job creation. That is nonsense. If the government had listened to my party's leader at the time of the last budget it would have cut taxes for this country's low income people, increased demand, and put our factories back to work. Instead of doing that, the Minister of Finance, on the advice of Mr. Bouey, Governor of the Bank of Canada, adopted the sort of policies Mr. Simon, United States Secretary of the Treasury under President Ford, adopted to fight inflation.
The government is trying to cure inflation by creating more unemployment, and the sad part of it is that it is not curing inflation, because it is getting worse. My authority for saying this is the projection of first quarters figures to which I referred earlier. Mr. Speaker, we must tackle both inflation and unemployment. You cannot argue simplistically that cutting income tax for lower income groups would so increase aggregate demand as to push inflation up. The government still thinks that too much money is chasing too few goods, and will not cut taxes for lower income people. On the other hand upper income groups already avail themselves of many tax loopholes, and if you increase their incomes you merely enable them to increase their personal savings. The people in the upper income levels are already increasing their savings, but the people lower down on the scale are not. We need to correct this.

But the government chose not to do this. It should have acted to bring interest rates down. It chose not to do this because it is imbued with the notion that our inflation is a result of too much money chasing too few goods. When will the government get it into its head that its policies lead to the underutilization of human beings, as measured by our unemployment figures, official and hidden, and the underutilization of manufacturing capacity?
The government would not have increased inflation if it had cut taxes for lower income people. In the face of slack demand prices would not have risen. As it is, some powerful corporations could well push prices up in future; and such inflation could be termed cost-push inflation, which must be tackled by other means.

Mr. Speaker, the government's policies have led to a deficiency of aggregate demand and deficiency of growth, and are causing a great deal of hardship. At the same time, they are not tackling the structural problems of the Atlantic region, and other regions, including Ontario and Quebec. When will the government get the message that you cannot continue to protect with high tariffs that are the highest in the western world, about 30 per cent? They were started under Sir John A. Macdonald in 1879 and have continued until 1977. Now the government is finding that this is beginning to catch up to workers in the textile industry and other areas.
The government kept postponing the adjustments that had to be made. Plants did not modernize in Quebec and Ontario. We are paying for it with higher costs. It is now necessary to have import quotas in order to keep the unemployment rate in Ontario and Quebec from going sky high. There are other forms of protective measures as well.
The structures in the Atlantic region must be examined. DREE policies are not doing the job. 1 raised this with the representatives of the Economic Council of Canada when they appeared before the DREE meeting. There must be new types of institutions to co-ordinate better the funds for development going from the federal government to the provincial governments in order that there will be an actual increase in per capita earned income in the Atlantic region, instead of maintaining per capita income as the criterion by which we should be judging growth in the Atlantic region. You cannot judge growth in the Atlantic region in that way. You cannot argue on a per capita income basis as proof of development.
There must be more than just transfers in terms of unemployment insurance into these areas. There must be jobs. The people there must be allowed to make a productive contribution to the Canadian economy. We must close the gap of earned income per capita. However, the government does not
July 4, 1977

think along those lines. It only suggests that possibly new institutional arrangements will be needed.
No one pretends that in a federal state where there is a division between the federal and provincial levels of government and the child of provincial governments, the municipal governments, that it is easy to do these things.
We have to get at the root of the problem rather than by just making transfer payments into the Atlantic region, whether through baby bonus grants, unemployment insurance grants or what have you. That is really only a band-aid approach. That might sound too socialist to some people; what do they offer alternatively?
