subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) should know that growth in the major metropolitan areas is buttressed by DREE at the expense of employment in the outlying areas. That is a situation in every province, starting from Newfoundland through to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and into Quebec, Montreal and possibly Quebec City, where the large areas are supplemented by DREE. 1 know this is so in the Atlantic region. There is recently an attempt to change this, but it is not a serious attempt.
This is contributing to the over-all unemployment situation in Canada. This failure of government policy to create more growth is causing the cyclical high unemployment that we have at the present time. It is failing to correct regional disparities with serious efforts to increase earned income per capita in areas such as the Atlantic region and Quebec.
Several members have raised this point. I want to emphasize it once more. A very serious problem exists for the young people of this country. I am not talking about kids, but about people who have finished grade 12. We do not have grade 13 in my area. These people would like to go to vocational or technical schools and on to other forms of higher education.
These young people cannot get jobs because there is not enough money in Young Canada Works. The minister stated with regard to job creation that we do not need to worry about the effects of the change of eligibility for unemployment insurance. He stated that with the changes he is now introducing the Canada Works grants to these areas will offset any loss. I wish to quote some figures for the benefit of the minister.
For the first quarter net benefit period of 1976 for Glace Bay, these was $1,744 million in unemployment insurance. By 1977 that increased to $2.18 million. In Sydney it was $4.21 million for the first quarter of 1976, and $5.02 million for the first quarter of 1977. I have not referred to areas such as Port Hawkesbury and Inverness in the constituency of the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen), but the situation is the same there.
Employment and Immigration
Active claimants for unemployment insurance for the first quarter of 1976 averaged 76 units of people. In Glace Bay last year there were 2,112, and for the first quarter of this year 2,260. Last year in Sydney there were 4,935, and 5,300 this year. This indicates a complete failure of the government's programs to create jobs in these areas. Why would they want to put more unemployment insurance money into those areas than money to create jobs? This is what the government has been doing with its LIP project, the son of LIP, Canada Works, and the son of OFY, Young Canada Works.
The minister solemnly stated in this House that Canada Works was different from LIP because it would create permanent jobs for 50 to 52 weeks of the year. It is true there is a difference between Canada Works and LIP in that there are two stages of Canada Works as opposed to one stage in LIP.
1 took down the figures the minister quoted. I found that the allocation to Cape Breton for the first part of the LIP grant was $349,000 for my constituency, $382,000 for the constituency of the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir), and $347,000 for the constituency of the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso.

speechtext:
If you want to offer patronage like you do, that is fine. In any event, that is not much money when you consider there were 14,445 persons on active claims at UIC offices throughout Cape Breton Island in February of this year. The total labour force for the Island was about 48,000. That means one in four was drawing unemployment insurance benefits and not contributing to the economy.
What is most discouraging is the fact that this does not even take into account all of the young people entering the labour markets who cannot find jobs and are not eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. This money does not even begin to tackle the problem of unemployment in that area. My allotment provided the equivalent of 43 jobs for one year, and the other constituencies will get the equivalent of 41 and 47 jobs for one year. This is terribly discouraging, especially in an area with a housing problem which is some 70 years old.
Houses in mining areas, for example, desperately need repairs, to say nothing of the need for at least one new coal mine in these times of increasing oil prices. So far as the housing problem is concerned, I wrote to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and he sent me back information about increases for all of Nova Scotia. In my letter to him I said this:
When the Hon. Barney Danson was head of your present department, he went to Cape Breton for a special meeting and personally told me that he was shocked at some of the housing that he had seen.
I have been trying to get the Cape Breton Development Corporation and CMHC involved in a special program for the mining communities are often left a legacy of old (about 70 years and over) company housing which I have often referred to as proletarian housing. They lack basements and many of them that are now owned by coal mine pensioners and/or their widows are going down the hill fast and are creating blighted areas in various sections of the mining towns.

July 4, 1977
Employment and Immigration
In fact, Mr. Speaker, incipient slum areas are being created. Continuing:
Enclosed is a recent copy of a letter which I sent to Mr. Matheson, who is presently the head of Devco. I cannot see why CMHC and Devco cannot get together to offer these pensioners and widows a special rehabilitation package. It would save a large problem for the future as I see it and would create jobs that are badly needed there now.
This is particularly so in light of the unemployment insurance figures to which I have referred.
A five to ten year plan would not be that expensive. I, personally, would like to see an experiment on this type of rehabilitation carried out over a five year period, with the worst homes being chosen.
Even though the pensioners are generally below $6,000 in family income, I would expect that they would have to make some contributions because I don't want such a program to be looked on as just welfare. Some of them may be capable of putting some sweat equity in but in any case they should be required to make some financial sacrifice in return for this effort.
Devco officials have, in the past, not considered this as a part of their obligation under the Cape Breton Development Act as I see it, though they are in the housing field to some extent already by holding an equity in Reeves Modular Homes (for the building of new homes). This is worth while but is totally beyond the ability of the pensioners and/or their widows to pay.
I wish you would seriously discuss this matter with Mr. Curran, CMHC manager in Sydney and with Mr. Matheson of Devco to see if we cannot get something started in the mining towns of Cape Breton.
The present NIP and RRAP programs are too slow and cumbersome to meet this need in an efficient way. In fact, I would go so far as to say, as I have in the attached letter, that for some of the mining areas of Cape Breton, and I am sure it would hold in other places that have an old stock of company houses, that having an area declared a NIP one before you can get RRAP funding, is putting the cart before the horse. The dominant need in such areas of old housing stock is home repair and neighbourhood improvement should follow, giving the people decent shelter.
I realize that you have all of Canada to think about but a slavish universal clinging to any federal program is one of the things that can get any federal state into difficulties. This is but one example of how this is happening in Canada today.
As I have said, there is more unemployment insurance being paid in my area than is required to provide short-term and medium-term jobs, such as constructing decent homes for the people over the next 20 years. This would create jobs in the construction industry and would have a multiplier effect on the economy as well as reducing unemployment in the area by perhaps 2 or 3 per cent.
I disagree with the hon. member for Hamilton West. The reason I am still opposing this change in eligibility is that we are not getting the guarantees which are shown in the first phase. Why should we leave people subject to the whim of government when we know that instead of spending money on unemployment insurance the government could spend it on creating jobs even for the short term? I suggest there is something seriously wrong with the co-ordination which should exist between the various departments. The finance department is, of course, talking outmoded economics. It is of the view that the prime cause of inflation in this country is too much money chasing too few goods-a demand-pull inflation. That is not why we have an inflationary spiral in Canada.
We can improve the cyclical unemployment picture by stimulating the economy. I hope there will be a budget this fall which will cut taxes for low income groups and reduce their mortgage rates by one or 2 per cent. At the moment there is a

moratorium on public housing in Nova Scotia because CMHC and the province cannot get together. As a result people are being pushed off into slum housing. The government is paying as much unemployment insurance in some of these areas as it is in some places in Newfoundland, and this is why the government should make a special effort to create jobs instead. In so doing it would be helping national as well as regional policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, frankly it makes me somewhat uneasy and perhaps somewhat embarrassed to talk about unemployment in a country as beautiful and as big as Canada, a country which is enormously wealthy and young and which has incredible potential. It is truly sad to talk about unemployment when there are underdeveloped and poor countries which envy us our wealth. They must think we are stupid not to find the answer to stimulate our economy and correct the present situation.
Mr. Speaker, unemployment can be considered a waste of human resources. Statistics Canada has given a rather dark picture of work possibilities for Canadians in 1976 and 1977. According to these reports from economists, Mr. Speaker, stagnation threatens several regions of our country and the social and economic effects of such a situation can no longer be ignored. Indeed, I have received in the last few weeks many copies of a petition asking for the withdrawal of the bill now under consideration, Bill C-27. Up to this time, approximately
6,000	people have signed this petition which reads as follows:
I, the undersigned, am opposed to the bill introduced by Minister Bud Cullen and denounce it as being unrealistic, misleading, discriminatory, catastrophic and reactionary, and demand instead the implementation of effective programs to fight against seasonal unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, it is true that the bill introduced in the House by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) on December 10 of last year contains some amendments which are important for all workers and unemployed in the country, especially in eastern Quebec and the Maritime provinces. Bill C-27 stipulates that from now on a claimant will need to have worked at least 12 weeks to be entitled to unemployment insurance, instead of eight, as the present legislation provides. Moreover, claimants having worked fewer than 25 weeks will of course be entitled only to an initial benefit period and will lose the right to benefits during the following periods: an extension period according to the period of unemployment, an extension period according to the national unemployment level, an extension period according to the regional level of unemployment, an extension period according to the gap between the national and regional levels of unemployment.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, our courageous workers are going to lose some benefits because of this bill as is indicated in the following data, an illustration which will give us an eloquent but rather frightening idea of what is going to happen, if this bill is passed. The eight-week working period, according to the present law, entitles one to 44 weeks of benefits. Under the new law, not a single week. Ten worked weeks entitles one to 44 weeks of benefits under the present law. But with the new
July 4, 1977

law, naught. Twelve worked weeks entitles one to 44 weeks of benefits, but under the new law, 12 weeks only. And so on and so forth, Mr. Speaker. As has been said before, the bill pretends to be realistic, and of course, it is the case as it is brought forward at a time when all our economists foresee an important slackening in our economic activities and a sharp rise in our unemployment level for 1977.
Misleading, because in the presentation of the budget they minimized the savings that the commission is going to make by insisting on the job creation programs without first ensuring that these very programs will affect the same unemployed people that are affected by the cutback. One can in fact foresee that the Canada Works Program will not really affect seasonal workers in the Gaspe peninsula, in northern New Brunswick, the fishermen and the people who work in the seasonal hotel industry and so on. It is discriminatory because it eliminates completely from the benefit of unemployment insurance all seasonal workers, married women, students who hold a summer job, yet do not qualify for the 12 weeks of employment even though they still have to pay their contributions to the unemployment insurance fund. This measure is catastrophic from an economic standpoint for the lower St. Lawrence region, the Gaspe region, northern New Brunswick and probably all the regions affected during those months when unemployment is at its highest level and the unemployment insurance will make savings of several millions of dollars through those cutbacks and that on the backs of the workers. It is a reactionary measure from a social standpoint because it will substantially increase the number of people on welfare given the absence of efficient programs to fight seasonal unemployment in the lower St. Lawrence and the Gaspe region.
Mr. Speaker, the present government insists on the fact that it has had to give priority to the fight against inflation even if that fight was going to contribute in a painful soaring of unemployment in Canada, an increase such as we have not known since the thirties. In fact, in my humble opinion, that is quite ridiculous, as I said previously, in such a vast and rich country as ours where so many things should be done whereby we could employ all the present unemployed people and still another million individuals. We would not even have enough people to fill the positions required to accomplish all the tasks which we should carry out in this country, such as building houses for middle income workers and senior citizens, such as constructing roads, improving the landscape, cleaning up all beaches, and what else. Mr. Speaker, it is not because there is no work to be done that we have unemployment, it is because the financial system does not meet the need of society in 1977.
Let us take as an example the shoe industry situation. In the last 12 months, 21 shoe manufacturing plants went out of business in Canada, which resulted in the loss of 2,500 jobs when we are now experiencing, as 1 was saying a moment ago, the highest unemployment rate in 37 years. Yet, what is the government doing to correct this situation? Nothing at all. They are making studies, they are studying and studying.
Employment and Immigration
Besides, when questions are asked, the answer is that the matter is under study. In other words, while fighting inflation, the federal government slowed down the economy which resulted in a very high unemployment rate, particularly in Quebec, even though inflation in this province has not been the main problem since 1967. Quite the opposite, the main problem is undoubtedly the economic revival and job creation.
In this context, it can easily be understood why an ex-minister of the Liberal government could say: "If we do not succeed in decreasing the unemployment rate, the number of revolutionaries will increase, and Quebec will not have enough police officers to control the number of people revolted by the present system." Mr. Speaker, official opposition members are probably right when they say that the action proposed by the government to fight unemployment does not give the expected results. Here is a study entitled: Data on unemployment 1960-1971. That review enables us to analyze the comparative unemployment situation in 1960, 1965 and 1970. Here is the average annual unemployment rate for each of Canada's five regions. In the Atlantic area, the rate was 7.6 per cent of total labour in 1970, 7.4 in 1965 and 10.7 per cent in 1960, under a Progressive Conservative government. In the Quebec region, the rate was 7.9 per cent in 1970, 5.4 per cent in 1966 and 9.1 per cent in 1960. This means that unemployment was higher in Quebec under the Progressive Conservatives in 1960. In Ontario, the trend is similar. A 4.3 per cent rate in 1970, 5.4 per cent in 1960. In the Prairies, 4.4 per cent in 1970, and 4.2 per cent in 1960.
In British Columbia, the rate was 7.6 per cent in 1970 as compared to 8.5 per cent in 1960, which was under the Conservatives. With such a poor unemployment performance,
I suggest the opposition parties are in no position to give lessons, and they should be the last ones to criticize the government for not solving unemployment.
Seasonally adjusted statistics for January 1953 to December 1971 provide the following unemployment data for the periods from 1959 to 1962, under a Conservative government, and 1968 to 1971 under the Liberals. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think 1 have quoted enough figures. I simply wished to emphasize that political parties, whether Liberal or Conservative, have no magic wand to stop unemployment and control inflation.
We in the Social Credit Party of Canada believe we possess this magic wand and even if other members have often made a mockery of us, the fact remains that if they have a better alternative, I wish these gentlemen of older parties would give us some indication about it, so that we can work on it. I suggest that up to now, only the Social Credit Party of Canada has seemed in a position to do something or advocated a policy likely to fight inflation while solving the unemployment problem. I can see some members opposite or on my far right smiling. Their smile is meaningless and apparently they are satisfied with the present situation and the distressing plight of almost 700,000 Canadians who are almost always unemployed. This does not seem to affect them.
We in the Social Credit Party of Canada want to ensure the economic freedom and security of each and every Canadian

July 4, 1977
Employment and Immigration
and for this purpose, we are proposing to the Canadian people to implement a system which is said to be a new one whereas I believe it has been experimented in several places, where it was quickly removed as were those who were administering it. One can say that the mover of this alternative comes from England and wrote a volume on the Social Credit philosophy in 1916. For many people, social credit is a monetary reform plan. This is obvious! This is why in these days when money or credit is scarce, the monetary reform they are advocating is so popular.
The Social Credit Party of Canada is more than that. It is a social credit and a philosophical policy, that is to say that social credit is a philosophy rather than a policy. However, whenever a problem arises at home, it cannot be solved outside the door. Therefore, this is why in the political field it is important to attempt to put everything in order. The expectations of the Social Credit philosophy can be defined as an association or the power of human beings living in society to achieve the desired results in order to meet their needs.
So, Mr. Speaker, the way things are going, it is obvious that the traditional parties are helpless. All they can do is try to put people to sleep with all sorts of nonsense and let the skunk grow, as I said not too long ago in one of my speeches. You get used to the smell and to the idea that nothing can be done about it and that it must be suffered until the skunk dies by itself.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say to the government that it is now faced with a sizeable challenge and that I think it should consider creating immediately more jobs, particularly jobs suited to the needs of the people, the working people and which would have the effect of allowing those people to regain their pride and dignity lost through idleness, and at the same time they could make their contribution to the unification and the harmony of a beautiful and great country. I dare believe that those few words will have the effect of making the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) think and that he will withdraw this bill, at least for the moment, because if it were passed as it is that would have terrible effects on the working class and all the people in my area and in northern New Brunswick.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to join my colleagues in opposing the measure before us. We have opposed this bill from the beginning because we have never believed, nor do we believe now, that the reason unemployment insurance benefits cost the taxpayers so much is because there are large numbers of people who do not want to work and are living off the system. We believe the reason there is more unemployment today than there has ever been since the end of the Second World War, or even since the great depression, is not because people are suddenly unwilling to work but because the economic policies of the government have helped to create unemployment and made it more difficult for people to find jobs.
I find it interesting that the major opposition to this bill has, from the beginning, come from members of the New Demo-
[Mr. Allard.)
cratic Party. I find it interesting that from among the 16 members of parliament who belong to the NDP only two, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) and the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), represent constituencies which have very large numbers of unemployed. My constituency has so few unemployed that the amount of money available under Canada Works and Young Canada Works is the minimum allowed for that type of program.
When the bill was before us last March stories appeared in the newspapers that Liberal members from the maritimes would vote against the government and bring about its defeat because the bill was so bad. Let me quote from the Globe and Mail of March 21, 1977-1 wish the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) would listen to some of the things he said back in March and compare them with his silence today, rather than sit talking to the minister as he is doing now. The report in the Globe and Mail reads:
Herbert Breau, Liberal member for Gloucester, said the group was concerned about worsening unemployment in the country, especially in the maritimes.
Then the article goes on to give the figures. I am not surprised the hon. member was concerned because, according to the Canadian Press:
The Atlantic provinces were the hardest hit, with unemployment rates of 15.1 per cent in Newfoundland, 13 per cent in New Brunswick, 11 per cent in Nova Scotia and 9 per cent in Prince Edward Island.
The story continued:
Mr. Breau said in an interview, "We may or may not vote against it, but we have communicated our serious concerns to Prime Minister Trudeau, Manpower Minister Bud Cullen and the four maritime ministers."
"We will wait for a definite answer from Bud Cullen before making a decision to vote for or against the bill when it comes before the House."
"My constituency has one of the highest unemployment rates in the country- as high as 30 per cent now-and these provisions will make the situation worse. I have to consider the welfare of my constituents."
Well, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has been conspicuous by his silence in this debate. Yet nothing has really changed. Nothing has been done by the minister which will be effective in helping the unemployed in the hon. member's constituency.
On March 19, 1977, a couple of days earlier, the Toronto Star carried a news story under a big headline "Trudeau Faces Revolt by MPs over Jobs Bill". The first paragraph read:
The Trudeau government faces a backbench rebellion if it insists on pushing through a bill to make it even tougher for jobless Canadians to get unemployment insurance benefits.
The report continued:
The government could fall if Newfoundland MP David Rooney gets the four other Atlantic Liberals he says are also opposed to the bill to join him in voting against it. The five, he says, have agreed that the bill is unacceptable to them in its present form.
Rooney says he is so disgusted by the harmful effects of Bill C-27 that he is prepared to risk Liberal defeat to down the measure, and already he has the support of enough colleagues to bring down the government.
Later in the story they quoted the hon. member for Bonavis-ta-Trinity (Mr. Rooney) as follows:
July 4, 1977

"The cabinet would have got the bill through by now if it hadn't been for us holding up our support", said Rooney. "We've been under tremendous pressure to give in. But if I voted for that bill I'd be a martyr to my party and a traitor to my constituents.
"Most Canadians think of the jobless as a minority-and often a lazy one. In my district, I believe they're a tragic majority, and a bitterly disappointed group of people who want to work. There just aren't any jobs for them."
Has there been a sudden upswing? Are there suddenly thousands of jobs in the Maritime provinces? Of course there are not, and there are no prospects. The government's own service-there have been official press releases and those we have been able to hear about because somebody in the government service has felt they were so important that the information must be disseminated to the public whether or not the public likes it-tells us that unemployment this year will be at least 8 per cent and closer to 9 per cent, and prospects for 1978 are even worse than for 1977.
But of course the hon. member for Gloucester, and I suppose the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity, will say, "But the bill is quite different than it was back in March. We forced the government to change things". As a matter of fact while my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, was talking, the hon. member for Gloucester, who was so opposed to the bill back in March, was interjecting. He was not getting up to speak in support of the bill and of course not saying those things publicly which supposedly he was saying privately back in March. He was not saying anything.

1 said at the beginning of my speech that in the city that 1 represent there is not the kind of unemployment that exists in the Maritimes or in Quebec, whose members, at least Liberal members, have been singularly quiet about unemployment despite the fact that they have a 10 per cent rate of unemployment.

Employment and Immigration
who came ten days ago to tell the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and myself about how unemployment was affecting them, is that there is a universal feeling that the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the UIC do not react very quickly, very sympathetically, and very effectively to problems such as unemployment. speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. member a question, with his permission, and I think he is giving it. Mr. Speaker, I hope you will not deduct the time of that long so-called question from my time. I will answer the hon. member. If he had waited a couple of minutes I would have gone over precisely that change.
Under the minister's compromise proposal, as I said, Canada will be cut up into 54 regions. I say that that will be a bureaucratic nightmare. It may give employment to some of the economists and statisticians who have been graduating from Canadian universities and cannot find jobs, but certainly it will not help the unemployed, and there is no one who should know it better than those hon. members who come from high unemployment areas, such as the hon. member for Gloucester.
Before I get away from the original proposal of the 12 week work period required for qualification to the present ten to 14 weeks, I want to remind the hon. member for Gloucester, and some of his constituents I hope, that under the proposal which he is supporting the variable period will be re-examined after it has been in place for a while and the qualifying period will increase to a uniform 14 weeks across the country after three years, unless it is specifically extended by parliament. In view of the record of this country under both Liberal and Conservative governments of being unable to lessen regional disparities, in view of the fact that the people of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and eastern Quebec continue to be far behind the areas of high employment in Ontario, B.C. and Alberta in terms of wages, and in view of the hon. member accepting the idea that three years from now a person will have to work 14 weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits, I say that the hon. member for Gloucester has sold out his constituents.

Some ten days ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and 1 spent a day hearing representations from some of our constituents about the employment situation as it affects themselves and people they represent. It is true that the situation is not exactly comparable to what it was in the 1930's. It is true that people are not actually going hungry these days, because we have unemployment insurance benefits, welfare, and old age pensions. However, there are people who are unemployed, even in areas with relatively low rates of unemployment. The unemployed are no longer the poor, the uneducated, and the native people. I want to put on the record some of the representations which were made to us. Mr. Don Posnick, a representative of the United Steel Workers of America, reported to us what has happened to members of his union in the last six months. They are organized, and they bargain for 32 plants in the area. The situation for those workers is grim. Usually when there was a lay-off in one plant, Mr. Posnick told us that the union was able to direct laid off workers to another plant. This year that is not possible. Co-operative Implement is down from 1,000 workers last year to under 500 now. The reason it has that many working is that the company is operating on a four-day work week. The Manitoba Rolling Mills at Selkirk laid off between 250 and 275 workers because of automation, and another 100 would have been laid off except that the union negotiated an earlier retirement plan which permitted long service employees to retire. They are down to 400 employees from the usual 700.
Allied Farm Equipment is down 50 per cent, from 200 workers to 100. Joy Manufacturing is down from 140 to 68, and that company is working a four-day week. Dominion Bridge is in the constituency of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. For years Dominion Bridge had a permanent sign asking skilled workers to apply for work. Jobs were available. Today that sign is down, and 125 people have been laid off. Manitoba Bridge closed for seven weeks in January of 1977. A total of 1,000 steel workers have been laid off. These are workers in the over 50 age group, and unless they were highly skilled, they were laid off. Mr. Posnick suggests that many of them will never get work again. Dominion Bridge has laid off 125 workers. People with 18 year's seniority were laid off for five weeks. Mr. Posnick said that many members of his union will exhaust their unemployment insurance benefits before they will find another job. Steel workers are not the only ones who find it difficult.
July 4, 1977

The president of this year's graduating class from the educational faculty of the University of Manitoba appeared before us. Ele told us that he surveyed 648 members of this year's graduating class. Over 60 per cent of them responded, and anyone who has conducted any kind of survey knows that that is a very large response. In June of this year, last month, when most school divisions had hired for next September, 56 per cent of those graduates who responded had not found a job either in Manitoba or outside that province, and 25 per cent of those who responded did not expect to get jobs this fall. That is the situation for the graduating class in the faculty of education. We are talking about a group of students who spent four years at university. That cost the people of Canada tens of thousands of dollars.
The Economic Council of Canada, the Department of Manpower and Immigration, and every other agency which was supposedly studying the needs of this country were urging young people to stay in school, to go to technical-vocational schools, to community colleges or to universities. We know that all the surveys which have been done show that a person with a university education earns a much higher income and has a much better ability to earn than people who have not gone to university. People who have gone to community colleges are able to earn a great deal more than those who have not. The young people of this country responded to those appeals. They went to universities and community colleges. Today they are coming out of those institutions, and there are no jobs.
The president of the graduating class of the school of social work at the University of Manitoba was unable to come to see us because she was ill, but I spoke to her and she told me that the job situation for graduating students at the school of social work is, to say the least, grim. She says that 50 per cent to 60 per cent of this year's graduating class have not been able to find permanent work.
I am glad that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) is in his seat. The president of the graduating class of the school of social work told me that the Canada Manpower office in Winnipeg has a terrible attitude toward students. The minister shrugs at what I say. I am just quoting what the president of the graduating class of the school of social work said. If the minister likes, 1 will be happy to give him her telephone number so he can find out whether I am quoting correctly. She said that the Canada Manpower office in Winnipeg has a terrible attitude, as though it were the fault of the students graduating in social work that there are no jobs. There are no jobs, not because there is no need for social work but because the federal government itself, and it has convinced all provincial governments, preaches restraint. What restraint means is fewer services, and that is achieved by helping fewer people. The needs are great but we are told to show restraint-to cure inflation on the backs of the unemployed. That is what we are doing.
Employment and Immigration
One of the most moving presentations I have ever heard in my political life was made by Sister MacNamara, the Director of Rossbrook House Inc. in Winnipeg, and I should like to quote from her brief. She referred to the fact that we have
900,000	potential members of the work force who cannot obtain jobs. She also referred to the fact that the ranks of the unemployed include skilled, semi-skilled, and professional personnel. She said:
Though the unemployment picture cuts across all age groups, the problem is especially acute among younger workers and those who are entering the work force for the first time.
These facts would be bad enough if they stated the worst of the situation, but the fact remains that the unemployment statistics conceal as much as they reveal. Statistics indicating rates of 7 per cent or 8 per cent never reflect the actual situation in areas of chronic, long-term unemployment, such as the inner cores of major cities. Whole groups are excluded from the statistics, status Indians and young workers being conspicuous among those who simply do not count in the eyes of statisticians. Few reserves boast unemployment rates of 7 per cent or 8 per cent. The actual figures would be closer to 40, 50 or 100 per cent. But reserves are never included in the statistics.
Of course that is true. That is how the unemployment rate is kept lower by probably half to 1 per cent than it actually is. She continued:
Similarly, school drop-outs, willing to work but with few marketable skills, have never been able to obtain a foothold in the work force and therefore are not counted in the unemployment statistics.
The result is that the unemployment statistics are seriously defective in terms of accurately documenting prevailing conditions, and the statistics are most conspicuously wrong when documenting those groups where unemployment is a traditional problem.
For the young worker, the unskilled or the marginally equipped, the jobs that exist are short-term. The lay-off syndrome dominates, with consequent damage to the morale of workers whose working lives are lived in six-week intervals.
This is a dedicated woman who works seven days a week.

ENERGY-SUGGESTION HOUSING MINISTRY MAKE LOANS FOR HOME INSULATION AS CONSERVATION MEASURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I raise this evening is the one I directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) on May 27. It related to the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, which has now been brought into better focus by the announcement which the minister made, together with his colleague, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), concerning a $1.4 billion insulation program. Mr. Speaker, nobody suggests that the $1.4 billion insulation program will not be of benefit to some people in Canada. The ministers announced, with the greatest of fanfare, grants of up to $350 to cover two thirds of the cost of purchasing insulation materials for attics, walls, basement walls and floors over unheated spaces, for owners or tenants of self-contained homes, whether detached, semi-detached or row housing.
Really, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is not aware or completely overlooks the fact that there is already in existence the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program which provides grants up to $3,750 for the same purposes. It is a much better program because it goes much further in providing storm windows, siding, plumbing and heating systems, and many other home improvements such as the installation of foundations and basements in addition to insulation, which is most important.

July 4, 1977
7286______
Adjournment Debate
RRAP provides for loans, of up to $10,000 to low income earners of $6,000 or less. They can have $3,750 forgiven. It further provides that for every $1,000 over $6,000 income they lose $250 of the grant. The loans are repayable in up to 20 years, adjusted to family income. The highest payment is around $80 per month.
This is the program that the people of Canada want, particularly those on low income, in order to insulate their homes. However, insulation is no good by itself. Let me quote some figures to support that statement.
Statistics Canada indicates that 898,000 Canadians earned under $3,000 a year, 729,000 earned between $3,000 and $5,000, and 880,000 earned between $5,000 and $7,000 a year. It has been proved that most of those people own their own homes. However, because of the high cost of living, they cannot keep them up. Most have only space heaters, no basements, and many have holes in the walls. How far would $350 go to provide insulation for which they have little or no use?
A good portion of the $1.4 billion should be directed to those in the low income brackets under the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Plan. That program has been in existence since 1973. The parliamentary secretary knows how many times I have asked here in the House of Commons about where the extra funds are. It is a good program, the best they ever produced, but there are not enough funds. However, they can find $1.4 billion to provide two thirds of the cost of insulation, when for the hundreds of thousands of home owners in the category I referred to the $350 will go nowhere.
I have a beautiful little pamphlet here. I could send it to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. It invites people to participate in the program and get a free grant.
When 1 look at the homes in Newfoundland, and the situation must be the same across Canada, those on low income cannot afford to repair their homes. They are already spending a fortune on fuel, something they cannot afford.
The minister should take a realistic look at these programs and compare them. No one objects to the $350 grant. However, those earning $6,000 or less require much more. There are also those who cannot work but still own their homes. There is no hope of them insulating their homes in order to conserve energy and save a little money.
I say to the minister and the parliamentary secretary that they should look at the value of the RRAP program and put a portion of that $1.4 billion where it will do some good. They will save more than the $50 million they expect to save under the insulation program and save it for those who need it, the poverty stricken in this country.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-USE OF WRITS OF ASSISTANCE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to bring forward a matter which I last raised on March 16, 1977, and on previous occasions, primarily with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), relating to writs of assistance and the decision of the Federal Court which severely criticized the granting of writs of assistance in connection with the enforcement of the Customs Act and other federal statutes.
I purposely let this matter lie for as long as I have to allow the Minister of Justice, whom I took at his word at the time, to have an opportunity of making the fullest possible investigation, in consultation with the Law Reform Commmission and officials of his department, regarding the continuation of the provisions which allow these writs of assistance to be granted. In effect they are unlimited and unspecified as to time and as to the powers which are available in regard to entering and obtaining evidence.
At the time I raised this matter on March 16 the Minister of Justice indicated to me that he was in fact reviewing the question; he said he was conducting a fundamental review of whether and to what extent writs of assistance should be continued in our law. 1 am sorry to see that neither the Minister of Justice nor his parliamentary secretary is here tonight. I am regretfully coming to the conclusion that the Minister of Justice, in regard to some of these important decisions relating to the civil liberties of Canadian citizens,
July 4, 1977

tends to fence on questions and to answer them in a general way by saying the matter is under review. Then he simply does nothing about them. I think that on a matter of such great importance the Canadian people require some indication from the minister at this time of what position he is taking with respect to the provisions which allow the issuance of writs of assistance.
It has been pointed out, both editorially and in the House by myself and my colleagues, that writs of assistance and the powers available thereunder in Canada are unparallelled in any other jurisdiction. I suggest it has been long argued by those concerned with the administration of criminal justice in this country that it is unfortunate that no statutory considerations are set out for obtaining writs of assistance. The lack of judicial discretion when issuing these writs, and the corresponding lack of criteria upon which they ought to issue, should be compared with the provisions relating generally to search warrants. For example, in Re United Distillers Ltd. (1946), 88 C.C.C. 338, C. J. Ferris, of the British Columbia Supreme Court, stated at page 341:
The law seems to be well established that in granting a warrant to search, the information before the magistrate must be of such a nature as to permit him to grant the warrant judicially.
At page 344 of the same report, he continues:
1 find that the warrant to search was issued without there being contained in the information sufficient material to entitle the Justice of the Peace acting in a judicial capacity to issue the warrant.
This judgment was quoted with approval in Schumiatcher v. A. G. of Sask. and Salterio, J. P. (1960), 33 W.W.R. 132. The case law has generally held that the issuing of a search warrant is not a mere ministerial act, but a judicial act and that the judge must exercise a judicial discretion. For example, in Rex v. Moore (1922), 63 D.L.R. 472, the court stated:
Clearly what the statute requires is not merely that the constable is to have information which justifies him in making an oath that he has reasonable ground for belief, and that the magistrate himself should be satisfied by information on the oath of an officer that there is (in fact and in truth) reasonable ground for belief upon which the magistrate, in his discretion, may grant a warrant.. .
There is a very substantial difference between the use of writs of assistance in Canada and their use in England. In the English cases the court always has the alternative of either granting or refusing the writ of assistance. In any case it is a very rare occurrence that a writ of assistance will be issued in England, and for the most part the writ is issued for the purpose of recovering possession of and preserving chattels.
In Canada writs of assistance are far more serious matters for they are not considered merely as remedial, but rather are used to enforce criminal and quasi-criminal legislation-all the more reason that these writs ought only to be issued at the discretion of the presiding judge on the basis of explicit criteria which ought to be carefully scrutinized by the court.
Adjournment Debate
I should like to quote from the book of E.C.S. Wade and G. Godfrey Phillips, entitled "Constitutional Law" at pages 366 and 367, which reads as follows:
The principle that a plea of the public interest does not justify a wrongful act was established by the eighteenth century cases known as the General Warrant Cases. The practice of issuing general warrants to arrest unspecified persons and to search property is said to have originated with the Court of Star Chamber. It is obviously a powerful weapon to assist an embarrassed executive to obtain material upon which to formulate changes against persons suspected of hostility toward the government. At a later stage the practice was authorized by the Licensing Act, 1662, for use by a secretary of state to prevent publication of unlicensed material, and such warrants continued after the lapse of that act in 1695. The General Warrant Cases arose out of the attempt of George Ill's government to stifle the political activities of John Wilkes and the publication known as the North Briton. Even at a later date the severity of the law against seditious publications was maintained largely by executive action, but the cases decided once and for all the illegality of general warrants and thus deprived the executive of a formidable instrument of oppression.
Writs of assistance were also an issue at the time of the American revolution and they have not been legal in the United States since that time. I appeal to the Minister of Justice to come forward and tell this House, and the country, what position the government intends to take with respect to-
